_about: Species records. One record per species; a species appears on every country page whose code is in `countries`. Population figures are the most recent published estimates from the cited assessments, not live telemetry — `pop.asOf` and `pop.basis` state the survey behind each one.

species.habitat: Savanna, thorn scrub and montane forest, from the Namib's edge to the Kenyan highlands.
species.note: A browser, not a grazer: the pointed prehensile upper lip is a hand for stripping twigs. Notoriously short-sighted and quick to charge, which is a poor defence against a rifle. Numbers fell from around 65,000 in 1970 to 2,410 in 1995; every animal alive today descends from that bottleneck.
threats: Poaching for horn destined for Vietnam and China
Habitat fragmentation cutting off breeding exchange

pop.basis: IUCN SSC African Rhino Specialist Group continental estimate

species.habitat: Formerly the floodplain grasslands of the Nile-Congo watershed; now a single guarded enclosure at Ol Pejeta, Kenya.
species.note: Two animals remain — Najin and her daughter Fatu, both female, both unable to carry a calf. The subspecies is functionally extinct. Its only remaining path runs through frozen sperm, harvested oocytes and a southern white surrogate, and no one has yet produced a live rhino this way.
threats: Poaching, which removed the last wild individuals by 2008
Reproductive pathology in both remaining females

pop.basis: Ol Pejeta Conservancy census — every individual is known by name

species.habitat: Short-grass savanna; a grazer with a broad square lip built for cropping lawn.
species.note: The great conservation success story that is now unravelling. Reduced to perhaps 50 animals in Zululand around 1900, it recovered to over 20,000 by 2012 — then the poaching wave hit. South Africa alone lost more than a thousand rhinos a year for five consecutive years.
threats: Concentration of the population in few reserves
Cost of protection outrunning tourism revenue

pop.basis: IUCN SSC African Rhino Specialist Group continental estimate

species.habitat: Closed-canopy rainforest of the Congo Basin and the last West African forest blocks.
species.note: Smaller, straighter-tusked and darker than its savanna cousin, and recognised as a separate species only in 2021. It disperses the seeds of more than a hundred tree species — some of which germinate almost nowhere else — so its loss quietly rewrites the forest that outlives it.
threats: Logging roads opening previously unreachable forest

pop.label: No agreed continental total. The 2021 assessment measured an 86% decline over 31 years.

species.habitat: Savanna, miombo woodland and desert margin, from the Okavango to the Sahel.
species.note: The largest land animal alive. Herds are led by the oldest female, who carries in memory the location of water in droughts that come once a generation — which is why poaching the biggest tuskers removes more than ivory.
threats: Escalating conflict with farmers along range edges

pop.basis: Great Elephant Census aerial survey of 18 countries, carried into the 2021 Red List assessment

species.habitat: Acacia woodland and riverine forest in South Sudan and western Ethiopia.
species.note: Giraffe numbers fell roughly 40% in three decades while almost no one was counting — conservationists call it the silent extinction. The Nubian giraffe, as the IUCN Red List defines it, survives only in South Sudan and Ethiopia.
threats: Civil conflict across the South Sudanese range

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Arid and semi-arid bushland of northern Kenya, southern Somalia and southern Ethiopia.
species.note: The one with the sharp-edged liver-coloured tiles separated by cream lines — each pattern unique enough that researchers identify individuals from photographs the way others use fingerprints.
threats: Habitat loss to settlement and livestock

pop.basis: Giraffe Conservation Foundation range-wide estimate

species.habitat: Semi-arid grassland and scrub in northern Kenya and a remnant in southern Ethiopia.
species.note: The largest wild equid and the most narrowly striped, with a white belly and huge rounded ears. Unlike plains zebra it forms no permanent herds — males hold territories around water, and females move between them.
threats: Loss of grazing and water to livestock

pop.basis: Grevy's Zebra Trust and Kenya Wildlife Service national census

species.habitat: A narrow band of arid grassland in north-eastern Kenya, near the Somali border.
species.note: The only living member of its genus — a lineage with no close relatives anywhere, so its extinction would erase a whole branch of the antelope family tree. It wears white spectacles around the eyes and has never been bred in captivity.
threats: Rinderpest-driven collapse in the 1980s from which it never recovered
Predation on a very small population

pop.basis: Hirola Conservation Programme and Ishaqbini Conservancy surveys

species.habitat: True desert — the sand seas of the Termit Massif and Tin Toumma, Niger.
species.note: An antelope that never needs to drink, extracting all its water from plants and turning its coat from grey-brown to near-white as summer comes. Splayed hooves let it walk on sand. Fewer than a hundred are thought to remain in the wild, nearly all in one Nigerien reserve.
threats: Oil exploration and its access roads

pop.basis: Sahara Conservation aerial and ground surveys, Termit & Tin Toumma National Nature Reserve

species.habitat: Sahelian grassland and desert scrub along the southern edge of the Sahara.
species.note: The largest gazelle, and the tallest — long-necked, chestnut and white, built to see a predator across open sand. Three scattered subpopulations remain, none of them large enough to be secure.

pop.basis: Sahara Conservation range-wide survey

species.habitat: Sahelian grassland and desert steppe; reintroduced to the Ouadi Rimé-Ouadi Achim Reserve in Chad.
species.note: Declared Extinct in the Wild in 2000. Between 2016 and 2023 more than 250 captive-bred animals were flown from Abu Dhabi to Chad, released, and left to it — they bred, and in 2023 the IUCN downlisted the species to Endangered. It is one of the few large mammals to have come back from Extinct in the Wild.
threats: Historic hunting to extinction in the wild

pop.basis: Sahara Conservation and Environment Agency Abu Dhabi post-release monitoring, Chad

species.habitat: Cold, wet montane bamboo and cloud forest above 2,000 m on Mount Kenya, the Aberdares and the Mau.
species.note: A chestnut antelope with a dozen white stripes and heavy spiralled horns, living where the forest is permanently dripping. Perhaps a hundred survive across four isolated mountain blocks — fewer wild animals than there are in zoos worldwide.

pop.basis: Kenya Wildlife Service and Bongo Surveillance Programme camera-trap surveys

species.habitat: Stony desert and arid grassland in the Danakil and the Ethiopian-Eritrean borderlands.
species.note: Its species is the ancestor of the domestic donkey, and this is the surviving Somali subspecies, still running wild in one of the hottest inhabited places there is. Grey with zebra-striped legs, it survives on thorn and coarse grass and can lose a third of its body water without harm.
threats: Hunting for meat and traditional medicine

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Equid Specialist Group assessment; no complete census exists

species.habitat: Afroalpine heath and grassland above 3,000 m — the Bale Mountains, Simien and five smaller ranges.
species.note: The rarest canid on Earth, and Africa's most endangered carnivore. It looks like a long-legged red fox and hunts giant molerats alone, though it sleeps and raises pups communally. Around 500 remain, split across seven mountain islands separated by farmland.
threats: Rabies and canine distemper caught from domestic dogs
Loss of Afroalpine habitat to barley cultivation

pop.basis: Ethiopian Wolf Conservation Programme range-wide monitoring

species.habitat: Savanna, miombo woodland and arid scrub; needs enormous ranges — a single pack may use 1,500 km².
species.note: Painted in blotches of black, tan and white, no two alike. Hunts by endurance rather than ambush and succeeds far more often than lions do. Packs regurgitate food for pups, for the old, and for the injured, which is unusual enough to be worth stating plainly.
threats: Rabies and distemper from domestic dogs

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Open grassland and arid savanna; ranges enormous distances and largely avoids protected-area cores.
species.note: Built entirely around one act: a semi-rigid spine, non-retractable claws and a rudder of a tail, for thirty seconds at 100 km/h. Three-quarters of the world's cheetahs live outside protected areas, which is why fences and livestock matter more to their fate than parks do.
threats: Loss of range outside protected areas
Cub trafficking through the Horn of Africa

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group range-wide assessment

species.habitat: Hyper-arid Saharan massifs — Ahaggar, Tassili n'Ajjer, Termit — where it hunts at night across bare rock.
species.note: Paler and smaller than savanna cheetahs, with a faint spot pattern and almost no mane. It is nocturnal, ranges over thousands of square kilometres, and is so rarely seen that camera traps went years between photographs.

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group; camera-trap detections across Saharan massifs

species.habitat: Savanna, open woodland and, in a few places, semi-desert; absent from closed rainforest.
species.note: The only social cat. Prides are held together by related females; males come and go on a few years' tenure. Lions have vanished from more than 90% of their historical range, and West Africa's population is now down to a few hundred animals in scattered parks.
threats: Trade in bones and body parts

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group continental estimate

species.habitat: The W-Arly-Pendjari complex spanning Benin, Burkina Faso and Niger, plus a remnant in Senegal's Niokolo-Koba.
species.note: Genetically closer to the lions of India than to those of the Serengeti, and reduced to a few hundred animals in one main population. Smaller, with sparser manes. Insecurity across the Sahel has made even counting them dangerous.

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: The most adaptable big cat: rainforest, desert margin, mountain, and the outskirts of cities.
species.note: Solitary, largely nocturnal, and strong enough to haul a carcass heavier than itself into a tree. Its adaptability disguises the decline — leopards persist at low density across huge areas, which makes losses hard to see until they are severe.

pop.label: No reliable continental estimate; the 2019 assessment documents loss of 48-67% of historical range.

species.habitat: Afromontane and bamboo forest between 1,400 and 3,800 m in the Virunga Massif and Bwindi.
species.note: The only great ape whose numbers are rising. Thicker-furred than lowland gorillas because of the cold and the altitude, and habituated groups are now individually known to researchers across three decades. The recovery is entirely the product of daily, expensive, physical protection.
threats: Disease transmitted by humans, including respiratory infections
Civil conflict in the Virunga landscape

pop.basis: Bwindi-Sarambwe 2018 and Virunga Massif 2016 sweep censuses, combined

species.habitat: Lowland and mid-altitude forest of eastern DR Congo, east of the Lualaba.
species.note: The largest primate alive — big males exceed 200 kg. Its range sits on top of the coltan and gold mining belt, and it lost roughly three-quarters of its population in twenty years while the region was at war.
threats: Bushmeat hunting around artisanal mining camps

pop.basis: Wildlife Conservation Society and Fauna & Flora range-wide survey

species.habitat: Rugged, steep montane forest along the Nigeria-Cameroon border — about a dozen scattered hill groups.
species.note: The rarest gorilla, and the most wary: it avoids people so successfully that most of what is known comes from nests, dung and camera traps rather than direct observation. Around 250 to 300 survive across roughly 12 fragmented localities.
threats: Isolation of subgroups from one another

pop.basis: Wildlife Conservation Society Cross River landscape surveys

species.habitat: Lowland swamp and terra firma rainforest across the western Congo Basin.
species.note: By far the most numerous gorilla — several hundred thousand — and still Critically Endangered, because Ebola and hunting have removed roughly 60% in a single generation and the decline has not stopped. Gorillas breed slowly enough that recovery from such a loss takes about seventy-five years.

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group range-wide modelling

species.habitat: Lowland rainforest south of the Congo River, and only there — the river has kept them apart from chimpanzees for over a million years.
species.note: Slighter than chimpanzees, with a centre-parted crown of hair. Bonobo society is led by coalitions of females, and conflict is defused with contact rather than violence. Lethal aggression between bonobos has never been recorded in the wild.
threats: Instability limiting protection across the range

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group; large areas of the range remain unsurveyed

species.habitat: Rainforest, gallery forest and, unusually, dry savanna woodland in Senegal and Mali.
species.note: The tool-using culture of this subspecies is the richest known: stone hammers for nuts, spears for bushbabies, caves for shade. It lost around 80% of its population between 1990 and 2014, most of it in Guinea, where the largest remaining population overlaps a major bauxite belt.
threats: Mining and infrastructure in core habitat

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group regional action plan survey synthesis

species.habitat: Moist and dry forest, woodland savanna and forest-farm mosaic across equatorial Africa.
species.note: Our closest living relative alongside the bonobo. Communities have distinct tool traditions passed between generations — some crack nuts, some fish for termites, some do neither despite having both the tools and the termites.
threats: Live capture of infants for the pet trade

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group range-wide estimate

species.habitat: Lowland and montane rainforest of the Cross-Sanaga region and Bioko Island.
species.note: A short-tailed forest baboon with a matte-black face ringed in white and, in dominant males, startling violet and scarlet hindquarters. Travels in groups of a hundred or more on the forest floor, which makes them easy to hunt in numbers.
threats: Commercial hunting with shotguns and dogs
Fragmentation of the remaining forest blocks

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group; Bioko and mainland surveys

species.habitat: Closed-canopy rainforest in the last unlogged fragments of eastern Côte d'Ivoire and western Ghana.
species.note: A striking guenon — black back, white bib and thigh stripe, and a long white beard. It is among the most threatened primates on the continent and may already be gone from most of the forests where it was recorded twenty years ago.
threats: Almost total loss of Upper Guinean forest

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group; Primates in Peril listing

species.habitat: Riverine gallery forest along a 60 km stretch of the lower Tana River, Kenya.
species.note: Confined to forest patches that depend on the river flooding — and the river has been dammed upstream. A leaf-eater with a chambered stomach, it cannot easily cross open ground between fragments.
threats: Loss of the flood regime that maintains gallery forest

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group forest-patch census

species.habitat: Montane forest on Mount Rungwe, Livingstone and the Ndundulu Forest, southern Tanzania.
species.note: Described in 2005 and placed in a brand-new genus in 2006 — the first new African monkey genus in over eighty years. Brown, with an upright crest and a honking bark. Roughly 1,100 exist, in two populations that have no contact.

pop.basis: Wildlife Conservation Society Southern Highlands census

species.habitat: Coral rag scrub, mangrove and the groundwater forest of Jozani, on Unguja island.
species.note: Endemic to a single island. Rusty red on the back, pale beneath, with a startled tuft of white around the face. Locally known as the poison monkey, an old belief that unexpectedly protected it from hunting for years.
threats: Loss of coral rag forest to farming and tourism

pop.basis: Island-wide survey published 2016

species.habitat: Cedar and cork oak forest of the Moroccan Middle Atlas and the Algerian Kabylie.
species.note: The only primate north of the Sahara and the only macaque outside Asia. It has almost no tail. Cedar forest — the habitat it depends on — is being lost to drought and grazing at the same time as infants are taken for the pet trade.
threats: Capture of infants for the illegal pet trade
Conflict where troops are fed by tourists

pop.basis: Range-wide survey of Moroccan and Algerian forest blocks

species.habitat: Eastern rainforest of Madagascar, from Anjanaharibe south to Mangoro — never below the canopy for long.
species.note: The largest living lemur, with a tail so short it looks unfinished. Family groups sing a wailing duet that carries two kilometres through the forest and is used to hold territory. No indri has ever survived long in captivity, so this species has no safety net at all.
threats: Hunting despite a strong local taboo

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group; no complete census exists for the species

species.habitat: Montane rainforest in a small block of north-eastern Madagascar, chiefly Marojejy and Anjanaharibe-Sud.
species.note: Entirely white, with bare pink-black skin on the face and a habit of leaping between vertical trunks rather than walking. Perhaps a few hundred to two thousand remain, none of them in captivity anywhere in the world.
threats: Hunting, which carries no local taboo here

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group range-wide estimate

species.habitat: Two tiny patches of dry forest near Montagne des Français, at the far northern tip of Madagascar.
species.note: Around fifty animals are thought to remain, which makes this one of the most endangered primates on Earth. Nocturnal, solitary, and small enough to sit in cupped hands, it spends the day wedged in a tree hollow.
threats: Charcoal production removing the last forest patches
A range measured in square kilometres

pop.basis: Repeated night-transect counts across the two remaining forest fragments

species.habitat: Fragments of eastern rainforest containing giant bamboo, chiefly around Ranomafana and Kianjavato.
species.note: Eats little except giant bamboo, including the shoots, which carry enough cyanide to kill a person. Believed extinct until rediscovered in 1986. Grey with white ear tufts and a powerful jaw for splitting culms.

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group site-based counts

species.habitat: Spiny forest, gallery forest and rocky canyon in the dry south and south-west of Madagascar.
species.note: The lemur everyone can draw, and one that is doing far worse than its fame suggests: perhaps 2,000 to 2,400 remain in the wild, fewer than are held in zoos. Troops are led by females, and males settle disputes by wafting scent at each other from their tails.
threats: Capture for the domestic pet trade and tourist photography

pop.basis: Range-wide site survey published 2017 in Primate Conservation

species.habitat: Rainforest, dry forest, mangrove and coconut plantation across much of Madagascar, at very low density.
species.note: A nocturnal lemur that fills the woodpecker's job: it taps a branch, listens for the hollow left by a grub, gnaws through with rodent-like incisors and hooks the larva out with a skeletal, ball-jointed middle finger. In parts of Madagascar it is killed on sight as an omen.
threats: Killing on sight where it is considered a bad omen

pop.label: Widely distributed but nowhere common; no population estimate has ever been published.

species.habitat: All remaining forest types in Madagascar, from spiny bush to montane rainforest.
species.note: Madagascar's largest carnivore and the only predator big enough to take an adult sifaka. Half-cat, half-mongoose in appearance, with semi-retractable claws and reversible ankles for coming down trunks head-first. Its closest relatives are African mongooses.
threats: Disease from domestic dogs and cats

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment based on density estimates across forest blocks

species.habitat: Bamboo scrub and dry forest around Baly Bay, north-western Madagascar — a range of a few hundred square kilometres.
species.note: The most valuable tortoise in the world by weight, and consequently the most stolen. Its high golden shell is so prized by collectors that field staff now deliberately engrave the carapace to spoil its market value. Fewer than a hundred are believed to remain in the wild.
threats: Collection for the international pet trade

pop.basis: Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust monitoring at Baly Bay National Park

species.habitat: Spiny forest and dry scrub across southern Madagascar.
species.note: Its shell carries fine yellow lines radiating from each dark plate — the pattern that gives it its name and its price. Around three million remain, which sounds safe until you learn the figure was twelve million in the 1990s. Single trafficking seizures have run to more than ten thousand animals.
threats: Mass collection for the pet trade and for meat

pop.basis: Range-wide density survey; down from an estimated 12 million in the 1990s

species.habitat: A handful of volcanic crater lakes near Bemanevika in northern Madagascar, plus a reintroduction site at Lake Sofia.
species.note: Declared extinct in the 1990s, then found again in 2006 when twenty-two birds turned up on a remote crater lake. Chicks were dying at three weeks because the lake had almost no invertebrate food; captive rearing and a move to Lake Sofia gave the species a second site.
threats: Loss of shallow marsh lakes to rice and sedimentation
Introduced fish eating ducklings' food supply

pop.basis: Durrell and Wildfowl & Wetlands Trust monitoring at Bemanevika and Lake Sofia

species.habitat: Lakes, rivers and mangrove-lined coast along the north-west of Madagascar.
species.note: One of the rarest raptors on Earth — around 120 breeding pairs. Pairs often nest as trios, two males to a female, apparently because good nest sites are so scarce. Unusually for eagles, the older chick almost always kills the younger.
threats: Loss of nesting trees and mangrove
Competition with fishermen and net entanglement

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Deciduous dry forest and, increasingly, open farmland in western Madagascar around Morondava.
species.note: The tall smooth-trunked baobab of the famous avenue near Morondava. The avenue is not a forest — it is what was left standing when the forest around it was cut, and almost no seedlings survive there. Adults may live a thousand years, so a stand can look healthy for a century after it has stopped reproducing.
threats: Conversion of dry forest to rice and pasture
Seedling loss to grazing zebu — regeneration has effectively stopped

pop.label: No individual count published; the assessment records an ongoing decline with almost no recruitment of young trees.

species.habitat: Steep, high-altitude native forest on Anjouan and Mohéli in the Comoros.
species.note: A black flying fox with orange eyes and a wingspan of nearly a metre and a half. It roosts in a handful of known trees on precipitous slopes, so a single cyclone can remove a meaningful share of the world population.

pop.basis: Durrell and Bristol Zoological Society roost counts, Anjouan and Mohéli

species.habitat: Native upland forest and gorge country in south-west Mauritius, plus the Bambous mountains.
species.note: In 1974 four birds were known alive, one of them a breeding female — one of the lowest points from which any bird has been brought back. Captive breeding and nest-box provision brought it back from the brink, though numbers have fallen again since. It hunts geckos among trees rather than hovering over open ground.
threats: Introduced macaques and mongooses taking eggs and chicks
Small gene pool from the 1974 bottleneck

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Remnant native upland forest and the fenced Île aux Aigrettes reserve, Mauritius.
species.note: Down to about ten birds in 1990. Intensive supplementary feeding and predator control rebuilt the population to around five hundred, but every bird descends from a dozen ancestors, and inbreeding now shows up as poor hatching success.

pop.basis: Mauritian Wildlife Foundation annual census

species.habitat: The Black River Gorges native forest, the last substantial native woodland on Mauritius.
species.note: The only parrot left in the Mascarenes; every other species there was driven extinct. Twelve birds remained in the 1980s. Nest boxes, disease management and thirty years of unglamorous fieldwork have taken it past eight hundred.
threats: Competition for cavities with introduced mynas

pop.basis: Mauritian Wildlife Foundation population monitoring

species.habitat: Native woodland and coastal plateau on five predator-free granitic islands in the Seychelles.
species.note: Reduced to a dozen or so birds on Frégate Island by 1970. Translocation to four more islands after rat eradication took it to roughly five hundred — a recovery that is entirely dependent on those islands staying rat-free.
threats: Vulnerability to a single reinvasion event

pop.basis: Seychelles Islands Foundation and BirdLife island censuses

species.habitat: Coral atoll scrub and 'tortoise turf' grazing lawns on Aldabra, Seychelles.
species.note: One of only two giant tortoise populations left on Earth, and by far the larger. Around 100,000 animals graze the atoll so heavily that they have created their own grassland — a dwarf turf of plants that fruit at tortoise height.
threats: Confinement to a single atoll vulnerable to sea-level rise
Introduced rats and goats, now largely controlled

pop.basis: Seychelles Islands Foundation atoll-wide counts

species.habitat: Offshore islands and two mainland colonies along the Benguela current, from Namibia to Algoa Bay.
species.note: Africa's only penguin, uplisted to Critically Endangered in 2024 after a century of decline. Colonies once numbered over a million pairs; fewer than nine thousand remain. Pairs bray like donkeys, which is where the old name came from.
threats: Collapse of sardine and anchovy stocks near colonies
Historic removal of the guano they burrowed into

pop.basis: South African and Namibian national colony counts underpinning the 2024 uplisting

species.habitat: Semi-arid coastal steppe and cliff ledges at Souss-Massa and Tamri, Morocco.
species.note: Black with an oily green sheen, a bare red head and a shaggy ruff — a bird that appears in Egyptian hieroglyphs and then almost vanished. Careful protection of the Moroccan colonies took it from Critically Endangered to Endangered in 2018. The eastern population is effectively gone.
threats: Hunting along the former eastern migration route

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Savanna, open woodland and — unusually for a vulture — the edges of towns and abattoirs.
species.note: The small, scruffy, thin-billed vulture that scavenges around West African market towns. It has declined by more than 80% in three generations, largely because it is deliberately poisoned or taken for belief-based use.
threats: Poisoning of carcasses, both deliberate and to kill other predators

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Open savanna and woodland across sub-Saharan Africa; nests colonially in tall trees.
species.note: Once the most abundant large raptor in Africa. A single poisoned elephant carcass can kill several hundred at once — poachers do this deliberately, because circling vultures show rangers where the carcass is.
threats: Deliberate poisoning of carcasses by poachers

pop.basis: BirdLife International assessment for the IUCN Red List; the species has declined by more than 90% in West Africa

species.habitat: Sahel and East African savanna, nesting on cliffs and escarpments.
species.note: The highest-flying bird ever recorded — one was struck by an airliner at 11,300 m over Côte d'Ivoire. It forages up to 150 km from the nest, which means a poisoned carcass anywhere in that radius reaches the colony.

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Seasonal wetland, wet grassland and adjacent farmland in eastern and southern Africa.
species.note: Uganda's national bird, crowned with a halo of stiff golden bristles. It is one of only two cranes that roost in trees, both of them African crowned cranes. Chicks are taken from the wild for private collections at a scale that alone would explain much of the decline.
threats: Illegal removal of chicks and eggs for trade

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Papyrus swamp and seasonally flooded marsh in the Nile and Congo basins.
species.note: A metre-and-a-half-tall grey bird with a bill shaped like a wooden clog, which it uses to seize lungfish. It stands motionless for hours and then strikes with its whole body. Its nearest relatives are pelicans, which is not obvious.
threats: Drainage and burning of papyrus swamp
Capture of chicks for the international zoo and pet trade

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Three tiny remnant patches of cloud forest on the Taita Hills, southern Kenya — around 400 hectares in total.
species.note: A small grey warbler with a black throat, confined to forest fragments that together would fit inside a mid-sized farm. Fewer than 250 mature birds remain.
threats: Almost total clearance of Taita cloud forest

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Mist-belt yellowwood forest patches in the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Limpopo, South Africa.
species.note: South Africa's only endemic parrot, dependent on old-growth yellowwood trees for both food and nest cavities — and those trees were logged out a century ago. Around 1,600 birds remain, counted each year in a single coordinated national census.

pop.basis: Cape Parrot Big Birding Day national simultaneous count

species.habitat: Dense riverine scrub along seasonal rivers in the Karoo, South Africa.
species.note: One of the rarest mammals in Africa, and among the least glamorous — a rabbit with a dark stripe along the jaw that lives in a narrow ribbon of vegetation beside dry riverbeds. Around 250 mature animals remain, and the females produce one kit a year.
threats: Ploughing of riverine scrub for crops

pop.basis: Endangered Wildlife Trust camera-trap and occupancy surveys

species.habitat: Renosterveld and fynbos lowland shrubland in the Western Cape — under 3% of it survives.
species.note: A small tortoise with a shell of black and yellow starbursts, restricted to one of the most heavily converted vegetation types on Earth. Fires in 2019 burned through several of the last populations.
threats: Near-total conversion of lowland renosterveld to wheat and vineyard

pop.basis: Turtle Conservancy and CapeNature surveys of remaining renosterveld fragments

species.habitat: Cliff ledges and steep escarpment grassland between 2,500 and 4,500 m in the Simien Mountains, Ethiopia.
species.note: Confined to a single mountain range, where it grazes on ledges that would stop most animals. Males carry heavy backswept horns ridged like a corduroy. From under 200 animals in the 1990s it has climbed back to roughly 500.
threats: Livestock grazing pressure inside the national park

pop.basis: Simien Mountains National Park counts

species.habitat: Afromontane woodland, heath and Afroalpine moorland in the Bale Mountains and Arsi highlands, Ethiopia.
species.note: Described only in 1910, the last large African antelope to be found by science. Greyish-brown with faint white stripes and, in males, gently spiralling horns. Almost the whole population lives in and around Bale Mountains National Park.
threats: Settlement and cultivation inside the range

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Antelope Specialist Group; Bale Mountains surveys

species.habitat: Wooded hill country, oak and juniper scrub in the Atlas ranges of Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia.
species.note: The only gazelle adapted to mountain forest rather than open plain — darker, stockier and with a distinct black face stripe. Nearly shot out by the 1930s, it has recovered slowly to around 2,000 in scattered Atlas populations.
threats: Overgrazing by livestock in mountain scrub

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Antelope Specialist Group Atlas survey synthesis

species.habitat: Savanna and arid scrub across eastern and southern Africa; shelters in aardvark burrows by day.
species.note: The only pangolin of the African savanna, and the one most often walking on its hind legs with its tail out as a counterweight. Pangolins are the most trafficked wild mammals on Earth — over a million are estimated to have been taken in a decade.
threats: Trafficking of scales to Asian markets

pop.label: No population estimate exists for any African pangolin species; trafficking seizure volumes are the only index of scale.

species.habitat: Lowland rainforest and forest-farm mosaic across West and Central Africa; climbs readily.
species.note: The most commonly trafficked of the four African pangolins, and the one most often found in West African bushmeat markets. It has three-pointed scales, a prehensile tail, and no teeth at all — insects are ground in a muscular stomach filled with swallowed grit.

pop.label: No population estimate published; seizure data indicate hundreds of thousands taken per decade.

species.habitat: Rainforest and moist savanna of Central and West Africa, from Senegal to western Uganda.
species.note: The largest pangolin, reaching 1.8 m and 35 kg. It walks on its knuckles with its foreclaws curled inwards to keep them sharp for opening termite mounds, and it is rarely seen — most records are from camera traps or from seizures.
threats: Forest loss to logging and agriculture
Very slow reproduction — one young at a time

pop.label: No population estimate published; recorded at very low density everywhere it has been surveyed.

species.habitat: Dense, closed-canopy rainforest of the Ituri and neighbouring blocks in north-eastern DR Congo.
species.note: The giraffe's only living relative, unknown to science until 1901. Striped hindquarters break up its outline in shafts of forest light, and its blue-black tongue is long enough to wash its own eyelids. It occurs nowhere outside DR Congo.
threats: Bushmeat hunting around illegal mining camps
Armed groups occupying the Okapi Wildlife Reserve

pop.label: No reliable total; the assessment records a decline of more than 50% in three generations.

species.habitat: Steep volcanic slopes and submarine lava caves between 150 and 250 m deep, off the Comoros and East Africa.
species.note: Known only from fossils and assumed extinct for 66 million years until one was pulled from a South African trawler's catch in 1938. It has limb-like lobed fins, a hinged skull, and a gestation of around three years — possibly the longest of any vertebrate.
threats: Very small population and extremely slow reproduction

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment; Comoros submersible surveys remain the main data source

species.habitat: Sea caves with underwater entrances along rocky Mediterranean and north-west African coasts.
species.note: One of the rarest seals on Earth, and a species that has retreated entirely into caves — it once hauled out on open beaches, and abandoned the habit under human pressure. Conservation work in Greece and Madeira helped move it from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2023.
threats: Disturbance and loss of cave habitat to coastal development
Disease outbreaks in the Mauritanian colony

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Forested rivers, lagoons and swamp creeks across the Upper Guinean forest belt.
species.note: A narrow-jawed fish specialist, recognised as a species distinct from its Central African relative only in 2018. It survives in scattered rivers that are increasingly fished with nets.
threats: Loss and pollution of forest rivers

pop.label: No separate count exists for the West African species since the 2018 split; the IUCN assessment published in 2014, made before it, estimated 1,000–20,000 mature individuals across West and Central Africa together.

species.habitat: Coastal desert, sandy gravel plain and salt marsh scrub along the south-eastern Mediterranean.
species.note: One of the smallest tortoises in the world — an adult female fits in a hand. It is functionally extinct in Egypt, where it once gave the species its name, and survives mainly in eastern Libya, from which it continues to be collected.
threats: Conversion of coastal desert to agriculture

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Tortoise and Freshwater Turtle Specialist Group assessment

species.habitat: Lowland rainforest and swamp on the Ujung Kulon peninsula, western Java — the entire world range.
species.note: One of the rarest large mammals on Earth, confined to one peninsula that sits in the shadow of an active volcano. Females are usually hornless. The last rhino outside Java was killed in Vietnam in 2010, which ended the species everywhere but here.
threats: A single population exposed to tsunami and eruption
Poaching — a 2024 investigation implicated an organised ring
Arenga palm crowding out food plants

pop.basis: Ujung Kulon National Park camera-trap census; a 2024 poaching prosecution suggests the true figure may be lower

species.habitat: Dense montane and lowland rainforest in Sumatra and Indonesian Borneo.
species.note: The smallest rhino and the only Asian one with two horns and a coat of reddish hair — the closest living relative of the woolly rhinoceros. Fewer than fifty remain in scattered pockets, and the animals are now so far apart that many females go years without meeting a male.
threats: Isolation of females who then develop reproductive tumours
Historic poaching that fragmented the population
Habitat loss to oil palm and logging

pop.basis: Sumatran Rhino Rescue and Indonesian Ministry of Environment and Forestry estimate

species.habitat: Alluvial floodplain grassland and riverine forest in Assam, West Bengal and the Nepali Terai.
species.note: Armour-plated in appearance because of deep skin folds, and a strong swimmer. Down to about 200 animals in 1900, it has been rebuilt to over 4,000 — Kaziranga alone holds more than two-thirds of them, which is the recovery's great strength and its main risk.
threats: Concentration of most of the species in a few parks
Severe flooding of Kaziranga in monsoon years

pop.basis: Joint India-Nepal population estimate; Kaziranga and Chitwan block counts

species.habitat: Grassland, dry and moist deciduous forest, and increasingly farmland edges across thirteen range states.
species.note: Smaller-eared than the African species, with a single finger on the trunk tip. Only some males carry tusks, which means poaching skews sex ratios rather than simply reducing numbers. More than a hundred people and several hundred elephants die each year in conflict along range boundaries.
threats: Habitat loss and blocked migration corridors
Capture for tourism and timber work

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Asian Elephant Specialist Group range-state synthesis

species.habitat: Lowland forest of Sumatra, especially Riau, Lampung and the Leuser Ecosystem.
species.note: Sumatra lost roughly seventy per cent of this subspecies' habitat in one generation, mostly to oil palm and pulpwood. Around 1,700 elephants remain in fragmented herds, several of which are now too small to persist on their own.
threats: Conversion of lowland forest to oil palm and acacia plantation
Poisoning and retaliatory killing in plantations

pop.basis: Indonesian Ministry of Environment and Forestry and WWF-Indonesia surveys

species.habitat: Mangrove, dry deciduous forest, rainforest and snow-covered taiga — the widest habitat range of any big cat.
species.note: Wild numbers reached a low of about 3,200 in 2010 and have since climbed past 5,500, almost entirely because of gains in India, Nepal and Bhutan. Southeast Asia moved the other way: tigers are now gone from Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam.
threats: Poaching for skins, bones and body parts

pop.basis: Global Tiger Forum compilation of national estimates

IN.basis: All India Tiger Estimation, National Tiger Conservation Authority

NP.basis: Nepal national tiger survey — nearly triple the 2009 baseline

species.habitat: Lowland and montane rainforest and peat swamp across Sumatra.
species.note: The last of Indonesia's three tigers — the Bali and Javan tigers are gone. Smaller and darker than mainland tigers, with narrower stripes and a distinct ruff. Around four hundred survive, and the Leuser Ecosystem holds the only forest large enough for a genuinely secure population.
threats: Loss of lowland forest to oil palm and pulp

pop.basis: Indonesian national tiger survey and IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group

species.habitat: Dipterocarp rainforest of Peninsular Malaysia, chiefly Taman Negara and the Belum-Temengor complex.
species.note: Down from around 3,000 in the 1950s to fewer than 150 today — one of the steepest declines of any big cat population. Snares set by cross-border poaching crews are the immediate cause; patrol teams pull thousands out of the forest each year.
threats: Forest fragmentation by roads and plantations

pop.basis: Malaysian National Tiger Survey (2016-2020) and subsequent government statements

species.habitat: Korean pine and Mongolian oak forest of the Russian Far East and north-east China, deep in snow for much of the year.
species.note: The largest cat alive, and the only one that routinely hunts in snow at -30 °C. Reduced to perhaps forty animals in the 1940s, it recovered under strict protection and now numbers around 600, with a growing population re-establishing across the Chinese border.
threats: Logging of Korean pine, which feeds its prey
Canine distemper crossing from domestic dogs

pop.basis: Russian national Amur tiger census; Chinese figures from Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park

species.habitat: Formerly the mountain forests of southern China; the IUCN range lists Jiangxi, Fujian, Guangdong and Hunan, each as possibly extinct.
species.note: Field surveys in 2001 and 2002 of eight reserves in five provinces, chosen as the places most likely to still hold tigers, found no evidence of one and concluded that no viable wild population remains. The subspecies survives only in zoos, and every living South China tiger descends from two male and four female wild-caught founders.
threats: Reserves of about 100 km², too small to hold even a few tigers
Forest converted to commercial tree farms
A captive population descended from only six founders

pop.basis: Sino-American field survey of eight priority reserves
pop.label: The subspecies survives only in zoos.

species.habitat: Temperate broadleaf and pine forest along the Russia-China border in Primorye and Jilin.
species.note: The northernmost leopard, with a coat that grows to seven centimetres in winter and rosettes spaced wider than any other subspecies. It fell to about thirty animals; a Russian national park and a matching Chinese one have taken it back above a hundred.
threats: Inbreeding in a tiny founder population

pop.basis: Land of the Leopard National Park camera-trap census plus Chinese cross-border monitoring

species.habitat: Remaining forest blocks on Java, from Ujung Kulon to Meru Betiri, including several volcanoes.
species.note: The last big cat on Java after the tiger's extinction there, and often melanistic — the famous black panther. It survives on an island holding more than 150 million people, in forest fragments that mostly sit on steep volcanic slopes nobody wanted to farm.

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Rugged arid mountains and wadis of the southern Arabian Peninsula, chiefly Oman's Dhofar.
species.note: The smallest and palest leopard, and the last big predator of Arabia. Its 2022 assessment counted no more than 84 mature animals, in Oman and Yemen; the best-studied population lives in Oman's Dhofar mountains.
threats: Prey depletion by hunting of ibex and gazelle

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Dry teak and thorn forest of the Gir landscape in Gujarat, plus surrounding farmland and coastal scrub.
species.note: The world's only lions outside Africa, all descended from perhaps twenty animals protected by the Nawab of Junagadh in the early 1900s. Smaller-maned than African lions and with a distinctive belly fold. They now number nearly 900 — and every one lives in a single district.
threats: Confinement to one population vulnerable to a single epidemic
Canine distemper, which killed dozens in 2018
Habitat pressure outside the protected area

pop.basis: Gujarat Forest Department Asiatic Lion Population Estimation

species.habitat: Arid desert steppe and mountain foothills of central and eastern Iran.
species.note: Once ranged from the Arabian Peninsula to India; now confined to Iran, where roughly a dozen animals are known to survive. Camera traps have picked up so few individuals that most are named and tracked personally.
threats: Road collisions on highways crossing the range
Prey depletion by poaching of gazelle
Killing by herding dogs and shepherds
A population too small to be self-sustaining

pop.basis: Iranian Department of Environment camera-trap monitoring

species.habitat: Alpine and subalpine rock above the treeline, from 3,000 to 5,500 m across twelve range countries.
species.note: A cat built for cliffs: a tail nearly as long as its body for balance, paws like snowshoes, and a nasal cavity that warms thin freezing air. It cannot roar. More than half the range lies in China, and much of it has never been surveyed properly.
threats: Prey depletion by competition with livestock
Warming pushing the treeline upward into its habitat

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group; total population including young estimated at 4,000-6,500

IN.basis: Snow Leopard Population Assessment in India (SPAI), the country's first national survey

NP.basis: Nepal national snow leopard survey, Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation

species.habitat: Mangrove, reedbed, marsh and tidal creek — wetlands rather than forest.
species.note: A stocky, olive-grey cat with partly webbed feet that dives for fish and taps the water surface to imitate falling insects. It depends almost entirely on wetlands, which are being drained and built over across South Asia.
threats: Drainage and conversion of wetlands to aquaculture

pop.label: No range-wide estimate; assessed as declining by more than 30% over three generations.

species.habitat: Peat swamp forest and riverbank vegetation in Sundaland — almost never far from water.
species.note: A small, oddly proportioned cat with a flattened skull, forward-set eyes and teeth adapted for gripping fish. It is tied to lowland peat swamp, which is drained and burned for plantations across Southeast Asia.
threats: Drainage and burning of peat swamp forest

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group; recorded from fewer than 100 localities in total

species.habitat: Upland forest of the Batang Toru ecosystem in North Sumatra — about 1,100 km² and nothing else.
species.note: Described as a species in 2017, making it the most recently recognised great ape and immediately the most endangered. Around 800 individuals survive in three forest blocks split by a valley, and a hydropower scheme sits in the middle of the largest.
threats: A hydroelectric development fragmenting the core population

pop.basis: Batang Toru nest-count surveys published with the species description

species.habitat: Lowland and hill rainforest of northern Sumatra, overwhelmingly within the Leuser Ecosystem.
species.note: Slimmer-faced and more sociable than the Bornean species, with longer beards on both sexes. Females give birth about once every nine years — among the longest birth intervals of any mammal — so every adult female killed removes decades of potential recovery.

pop.basis: Range-wide nest survey and habitat modelling, Leuser Ecosystem

species.habitat: Lowland dipterocarp, peat swamp and hill forest across Borneo.
species.note: Around 104,700 remain — a large number that hides the shape of the problem: more than 100,000 were lost between 1999 and 2015, and the species is projected to fall by nearly 90% across three generations. Males develop broad cheek flanges only if they achieve dominance.
threats: Conversion of forest to oil palm and pulpwood
Killing during conflict and capture of infants

pop.basis: Borneo-wide density modelling published in Current Biology (2018)

species.habitat: A single patch of montane rainforest in Bawangling National Nature Reserve, Hainan Island, China.
species.note: The rarest primate on Earth. Down to nine animals in the 1970s, it now numbers around forty-two in seven family groups, all within one valley. Males are black, females golden. Rope bridges have been strung across a landslide gap to reconnect their canopy.
threats: A world population confined to one forest patch
No genetic exchange with any other population

pop.basis: Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden and Hainan Bawangling annual group census

species.habitat: A single block of degraded karst forest straddling the Vietnam-China border in Cao Bang and Guangxi.
species.note: Believed extinct until rediscovered in 2002 in a strip of limestone forest a few kilometres wide. Around 135 animals remain in the only population, which is now protected on both sides of the border by a rare transboundary agreement.
threats: A single population on fragile karst
Firewood collection and grazing degrading the forest

pop.basis: Fauna & Flora joint Vietnam-China simultaneous census

species.habitat: Steep limestone karst forest in Ha Giang and Tuyen Quang provinces, northern Vietnam.
species.note: Black and cream with pale blue face patches, thick pink lips and an upturned nose. Thought extinct until 1989. Around 250 remain in a handful of karst blocks, the largest holding perhaps 130.
threats: Hunting for meat and traditional medicine
Karst forest loss to quarrying and firewood

pop.basis: Fauna & Flora Vietnam karst-block surveys

species.habitat: Limestone cliffs and karst forest of Cat Ba Island in Ha Long Bay, Vietnam.
species.note: Golden-headed, black-bodied, and confined to one island. Hunting for traditional medicine cut it from around 2,800 in the 1960s to 53 by 2000. Strict protection has slowly lifted it back above eighty — one of the smallest populations of any primate to have turned a corner.
threats: Isolation of subgroups by cliffs and water

pop.basis: Cat Ba Langur Conservation Project annual census

species.habitat: Limestone karst forest in Van Long and a handful of other reserves in northern Vietnam.
species.note: Black with a broad white 'trouser' patch across the rump and thighs. Around 250 survive in nineteen isolated subpopulations, only two of which contain more than fifty animals.

pop.basis: Fauna & Flora and Endangered Primate Rescue Center monitoring

species.habitat: Fir and larch forest between 3,000 and 4,500 m in the Yunling range of north-west Yunnan and south-east Tibet.
species.note: Lives higher than any other non-human primate, eating mostly lichen from conifers because little else grows there in winter. Pink-lipped and expressive, with a nose so flattened it appears to have none.
threats: Logging of old-growth fir, which carries the lichen it eats

pop.basis: Chinese Academy of Sciences and Fauna & Flora range-wide troop counts

species.habitat: Wet evergreen rainforest of the Western Ghats, between about 600 and 1,500 m.
species.note: A black macaque with a great silver mane and a tufted tail like a lion's. It is a canopy specialist that will not cross open ground, so a road through its forest divides a population permanently.
threats: Fragmentation of Western Ghats rainforest by tea and coffee estates

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group; Western Ghats fragment censuses

species.habitat: Montane and lowland forest, bamboo and plantation edge on Java.
species.note: One of the only venomous primates: it draws toxin from a gland inside its elbow into its mouth. Traders pull the teeth out with nail clippers before selling them as pets, and most animals die of infection before reaching a buyer.
threats: Capture for the domestic and online pet trade
Injury and infection from having teeth removed

pop.label: No population estimate published; the assessment records an ongoing decline exceeding 80% over three generations.

species.habitat: Forest in the Annamite Mountains of Vietnam and Laos.
species.note: Discovered by Western science only in 1992, in the Annamite Mountains between Vietnam and Laos, and never counted. The last confirmed record is a camera-trap photograph taken in central Vietnam in 2013, and the IUCN marks its own assessment as needing an update. Since April 2025 a team with detection dogs and a rapid DNA test has been searching 300 km² of Bolikhamxay province in Laos for survivors.
threats: Conversion of forest to crops and plantations

pop.label: The IUCN's 2015 assessment allows 25–750 mature individuals, most likely 50–300; in 2021 IUCN experts put realistic numbers below 100. None has been confirmed since 2013.

species.habitat: Gobi desert gravel plain and salt pan in the Lop Nur and Great Gobi 'A' reserves.
species.note: A separate species from the domestic Bactrian, not merely a feral form. It can drink salt water, and the Lop Nur population persisted through decades of nuclear weapons testing there. Fewer than 1,400 mature animals remain, in China and Mongolia.
threats: Competition with domestic camels and interbreeding

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Semi-desert steppe and grassland in Mongolia and Xinjiang, China; reintroduced herds also roam in Kazakhstan, and a free-living herd has settled in the Chernobyl exclusion zone.
species.note: The last wild horse — never domesticated, and with 66 chromosomes rather than the domestic horse's 64. It went extinct in the wild in the 1960s and every animal alive descends from twelve founders. Reintroduction began in 1992 and there are now free-ranging herds again in Mongolia.
threats: An entire species descended from twelve founders

pop.basis: International Takhi Group and global studbook; several hundred are free-ranging in Mongolia and China

species.habitat: Open steppe and semi-desert in Kazakhstan, Kalmykia and western Mongolia.
species.note: A Pleistocene survivor with an inflatable, drooping nose that filters dust and warms winter air. In 2015 a bacterial outbreak killed more than 200,000 in three weeks. And yet: Kazakhstan's herd has since grown past two million, and in 2023 the IUCN moved it from Critically Endangered to Near Threatened — one of the largest recoveries ever recorded for a mammal.
threats: Mass die-offs from Pasteurella outbreaks in hot, humid conditions

pop.basis: Kazakhstan national aerial survey; the 2023 Red List reassessment cites the recovery explicitly

species.habitat: Riverine forest and alpine meadow of the Dachigam valley in Kashmir, India.
species.note: The only surviving Asiatic subspecies of red deer in India, and effectively confined to one valley. Stags carry heavy antlers with five tines. Around 289 remain, up slightly from a low of about 170.
threats: Loss of the migration route to upper pastures

pop.basis: Jammu & Kashmir Department of Wildlife Protection Hangul census, Dachigam National Park

species.habitat: Grassland and forest on the slopes of Mount Iglit-Baco, Mindoro, Philippines.
species.note: A dwarf buffalo found only on Mindoro, with short V-shaped horns and a stocky build. It fell from around 10,000 in 1900 to under 200 by the 1980s, largely through rinderpest and hunting; strict protection has brought it back to roughly 480.
threats: Conflict between park protection and indigenous land use

pop.basis: Philippine Department of Environment and Natural Resources annual Tamaraw count, Mounts Iglit-Baco

species.habitat: Alluvial grassland, swamp and riverine forest, chiefly in Assam and the Koshi Tappu wetland of Nepal.
species.note: Carries the widest horn spread of any living bovid — up to two metres tip to tip. Perhaps 3,400 genuinely wild animals remain, and the greatest threat is not hunting but interbreeding with the domestic buffalo it gave rise to.

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Asian Wild Cattle Specialist Group; most animals are in Assam

species.habitat: Open dry forest, bamboo and forest clearings across Southeast Asia and Java.
species.note: A wild ox with a white rump patch and white stockings; bulls are blue-black, cows chestnut. Numbers have fallen by more than 80% and it is now gone from most of Indochina, brought down mainly by snaring rather than habitat loss.
threats: Snaring and hunting for meat and horns

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Asian Wild Cattle Specialist Group range-wide estimate

species.habitat: Lowland and hill rainforest of Peninsular Malaysia, southern Thailand and Sumatra.
species.note: Black at both ends and white in the middle — a pattern that reads as a broken shape rather than an animal in moonlit forest. Calves are striped and spotted like a watermelon. It has a short prehensile trunk and is the only Old World tapir.

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Tapir Specialist Group range-wide estimate

species.habitat: Dry and moist deciduous forest, alpine steppe and rainforest, from India to Java.
species.note: The Asiatic wild dog — russet, bushy-tailed, and living in packs of a dozen or more that whistle to keep contact in thick forest. Fewer than 2,500 mature animals remain, which is fewer than tigers, and almost nobody works on them.

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Canid Specialist Group range-wide assessment

species.habitat: Temperate broadleaf and conifer forest with a bamboo understorey, between 2,200 and 4,800 m in the Himalaya.
species.note: Not a panda and not a raccoon — the only living member of its own family, with a false thumb for gripping bamboo and a tail ringed like a lemur's. Fewer than 10,000 mature animals remain across a thin band of Himalayan forest.
threats: Forest clearance and livestock grazing removing bamboo
Poaching for pelts and the pet trade
Fragmentation of the Himalayan forest belt

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment; the total is thought to have halved in three generations

species.habitat: Montane conifer forest with dense bamboo understorey in Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu.
species.note: A bear that gave up meat for a plant it digests badly, and so must eat for fourteen hours a day. China's reserve network and reforestation lifted the wild population past 1,800 and earned a downlisting from Endangered in 2016 — the most-cited example of what sustained state investment can do.
threats: Fragmentation of bamboo forest by roads and settlement
Climate shifting the bamboo belt uphill

pop.basis: China's Fourth National Giant Panda Survey

species.habitat: The driest part of the Gobi desert — Great Gobi 'A' Strictly Protected Area, and nowhere else on Earth.
species.note: The only bear that lives in true desert. Around forty remain, subsisting on wild rhubarb, roots and berries near a handful of springs, and they are supplementary-fed through spring because the springs no longer reliably deliver.
threats: A world population of roughly forty animals

pop.basis: Mongolian Gobi Bear Project DNA hair-snare census

statusSource.text: Listed as Critically Endangered in the Mongolian Red List of Mammals (2006) under criterion D, fewer than 50 mature individuals.
statusSource.iucnNote: the IUCN Red List assesses the brown bear as a whole, as Least Concern

species.habitat: Subtropical broadleaf forest, bamboo and grassland from Nepal to Taiwan.
species.note: Declined by an estimated 90% in China alone. Its scales are keratin — chemically the same as fingernails — and are nonetheless traded by the tonne for traditional medicine. It digs burrows several metres deep and raises one pup at a time.

pop.label: No population estimate exists; the assessment records a decline exceeding 80% over three generations.

species.habitat: Lowland forest, secondary growth and plantation across Sundaland and mainland Southeast Asia.
species.note: The most heavily trafficked mammal in the region. Single shipping containers have been intercepted holding more than fourteen tonnes of scales — the remains of tens of thousands of animals. It curls into a ball when threatened, which works against leopards and not at all against a person with a sack.
threats: Industrial-scale trafficking to China and Vietnam

pop.label: No population estimate exists; seizure records indicate hundreds of thousands trafficked per decade.

species.habitat: Dry deciduous forest, scrub and farmland across the Indian subcontinent.
species.note: Larger-scaled than its eastern relatives, with a tail so heavy it can stand on it. India records hundreds of seizures a year, and the animals are increasingly taken to order rather than opportunistically.
threats: Trafficking networks reaching from village to border

pop.label: No population estimate exists; assessed as declining by more than 50% over three generations.

species.habitat: Lowland forest, grassland and agricultural mosaic on Palawan and nearby islands.
species.note: Endemic to the Palawan faunal region and recognised as a distinct species only in 2005. Trafficking to Chinese and Vietnamese markets increased sharply once mainland pangolin populations were exhausted.
threats: Loss of lowland forest on Palawan

pop.label: No population estimate exists; the assessment infers a decline of 80-95% over three generations.

species.habitat: The main channel of the Yangtze River and the connected Poyang and Dongting lakes.
species.note: The only freshwater porpoise in the world, and the last cetacean in the Yangtze after the baiji was declared functionally extinct in 2007. It has no dorsal fin and a mouth curved into what looks like a smile. A ten-year fishing ban has, unexpectedly, worked: the 2022 survey found 1,249 — the first rise ever recorded.

pop.basis: Chinese Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs basin-wide Yangtze survey

species.habitat: Coastal brackish water, estuaries and three great rivers — the Mekong, Mahakam and Ayeyarwady.
species.note: Round-headed, with no beak and a permanently amiable expression. In Myanmar, dolphins and fishermen have cooperated for generations: the dolphins herd fish into the nets and take their share. The Mekong subpopulation is down to about ninety animals.

pop.label: No global total; the Mekong subpopulation is Critically Endangered at roughly 89 animals.

species.habitat: Rivers of the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna basin and the Karnaphuli–Sangu system, in India, Nepal and Bangladesh.
species.note: Functionally blind — it has no lens — and swims on its side, trailing one flipper along the riverbed and navigating entirely by sonar. India's first nationwide survey, published in 2025, counted 6,324 of them and gave the species its first real baseline.
threats: Dams and barrages fragmenting the river

pop.basis: Government of India first national river dolphin survey, Wildlife Institute of India
pop.label: The survey counted 6,327 river dolphins across the Ganga basin: 6,324 Ganges river dolphins and three Indus river dolphins in the Beas.

species.habitat: A 1,000 km stretch of the lower Indus between the Chashma and Kotri barrages, Pakistan.
species.note: Split from the Ganges dolphin as a full species in 2021. Barrages built for irrigation cut its range into isolated sections and reduced it to around 1,200 by the 1990s; community-led rescue of stranded animals in canals has since taken it near 2,000.
threats: Barrages dividing the population into isolated segments

pop.basis: Pakistan Sindh Wildlife Department and WWF-Pakistan Indus survey

species.habitat: Shallow coastal seagrass meadows, from East Africa to Vanuatu.
species.note: The only herbivorous mammal that lives entirely at sea, and the origin of the mermaid story. It eats seagrass whole, roots included, leaving winding furrows on the seabed. Australia holds most of the world's dugongs; several other subpopulations are down to a few dozen.
threats: Loss of seagrass to coastal development and runoff
Hunting in parts of the range

pop.label: No global total. Australia holds tens of thousands; several regional subpopulations number under 250 and are separately Critically Endangered.

species.habitat: Primary dipterocarp rainforest on Luzon, Samar, Leyte and Mindanao, from lowland to 1,800 m.
species.note: One of the largest eagles in the world, with a two-metre wingspan and a shaggy cream crest it raises like a lion's mane. A breeding pair needs some 7,000 hectares of old-growth forest and raises one chick every two years.
threats: Loss of old-growth rainforest to logging and agriculture
Shooting, still the leading cause of known deaths

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Open dry grassland and thorn scrub in Rajasthan, Gujarat and a few remnant Deccan pockets.
species.note: A metre-tall grassland bird that nearly became India's national bird. Around 150 remain. The immediate killer is now power lines: the birds have poor frontal vision, fly heavily, and cannot swerve — collisions kill an estimated fraction of the population every year.
threats: Collision with high-tension power lines crossing the desert
Conversion of grassland to irrigated crops and solar farms

pop.basis: Wildlife Institute of India and BNHS surveys; Desert National Park counts

species.habitat: Lowland alluvial grassland — the Terai of India and Nepal, and the Tonle Sap floodplain of Cambodia.
species.note: A small bustard whose males leap vertically from the grass in a display flight, then parachute down on black wings. Its habitat is the most fertile land in the region, so almost all of it has been converted to dry-season rice.
threats: Conversion of floodplain grassland to intensive rice
Grassland burning during the breeding season

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Breeds on coastal tundra in Chukotka; winters on intertidal mudflats from the Yellow Sea to Myanmar.
species.note: A wader the size of a sparrow with a bill flattened into a small spatula, which it sweeps sideways through wet mud. It flies 8,000 km each way between Arctic Russia and the Bay of Bengal, and the mudflats it depends on halfway are being reclaimed.
threats: Reclamation of Yellow Sea intertidal mudflats
Hunting with mist nets on the wintering grounds

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Open country, villages and dry forest across the Indian subcontinent and mainland Southeast Asia.
species.note: In 1985 this was plausibly the most abundant large raptor on Earth. Within fifteen years, 99.9% were gone — killed by diclofenac, a veterinary painkiller given to cattle that causes renal failure in any vulture that feeds on the carcass. India banned its veterinary use in 2006, and the decline has since slowed.
threats: Residual veterinary diclofenac and other toxic NSAIDs in cattle carcasses

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Cliffs, ruins and old buildings in the drier parts of peninsular India and Pakistan.
species.note: The long-billed vulture, hit by the same diclofenac collapse that took the white-rumped: a fall of more than 97% in a decade. India's captive breeding centres now hold a genetic reserve, and releases into 'vulture safe zones' have begun.
threats: Veterinary NSAID residues in livestock carcasses
Loss of nesting cliffs and old buildings

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Wooded hills beside rice paddy and shallow marsh in Shaanxi, China, and reintroduction sites on Sado Island, Japan.
species.note: In 1981 seven birds were found in one Chinese valley — the entire species. Every crested ibis alive descends from them. Careful nest guarding, paddy management and reintroduction to Japan and Korea have taken the population past seven thousand.
threats: A gene pool descended from seven individuals
Pesticide use in the paddies it feeds in

pop.basis: Chinese State Forestry Administration and Japanese Ministry of Environment counts, wild and released birds combined

species.habitat: Breeds on Arctic tundra bog in Yakutia; winters on the shallow margins of Poyang Lake, China.
species.note: Pure white with black primaries and a bare crimson face, and the most water-dependent of all cranes — it feeds, nests and roosts in shallow water. The western population is down to a handful of birds; almost the entire species now winters on one Chinese lake.
threats: Dependence on a single wintering site at Poyang Lake
Hydrological change from Three Gorges Dam operation
Hunting on the western migration route

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International
pop.label: The assessment rests on a count of 3,750 at Poyang Lake in 2008 and 3,400 at Momoge in 2011.

species.habitat: Reedbed marsh in Hokkaido, the Amur basin and the Yellow Sea coastal wetlands.
species.note: The crane of Japanese screens and origami, and the second-rarest crane in the world. The Hokkaido population is resident and fed through winter; the mainland migratory population is falling as coastal wetlands are reclaimed.
threats: Reclamation of Yellow Sea coastal wetland
Dependence on supplementary feeding in Japan

pop.basis: International Crane Foundation flyway counts; total population near 3,050 including immatures

species.habitat: Dry monsoon scrub and savanna woodland in West Bali National Park and on Nusa Penida.
species.note: Snow-white with black wingtips and a bare cobalt mask — so ornamental that trapping for the cage-bird trade took the wild population to six birds in 2001. Release programmes have rebuilt it to a few hundred, and poaching from the release sites still occurs.
threats: Trapping for the Indonesian cage-bird trade
Nest cavity competition with introduced starlings

pop.basis: West Bali National Park and Nusa Penida post-release monitoring

species.habitat: Lowland and hill dipterocarp rainforest in Sundaland and southern Myanmar.
species.note: The only hornbill with a solid casque rather than a hollow one — a block of keratin the traders call 'red ivory', which is carved and sells for more per gram than elephant ivory. Males use it in aerial head-to-head jousts. Its call is a series of hoots accelerating into maniacal laughter.
threats: Targeted poaching for the casque trade
Loss of the tall trees it nests in
Slow reproduction — one chick, sealed in a nest cavity for months

pop.label: No population estimate published; assessed as declining rapidly under sustained targeted poaching.

species.habitat: Breeds on wooded lakes in the Amur basin; winters on lakes and reservoirs in eastern and southern China.
species.note: A diving duck with a green-glossed black head that has vanished from most of its range within a single human generation. Perhaps a few hundred remain, and the breeding grounds that once held it now have almost none.
threats: Loss of shallow lake and marsh habitat

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Deep, fast-flowing stretches of the Chambal, Girwa, Gandak and Rapti rivers with sandbanks for nesting.
species.note: A crocodilian with a jaw like a pair of tongs, holding more than a hundred interlocking teeth, used for catching fish and nothing else. Males grow a bulbous nasal 'ghara'. It fell to under 200 adults in the 1970s; the Chambal now holds most of the world's population.
threats: Loss of sandbanks to sand mining
Dams and barrages altering river flow

pop.basis: National Chambal Sanctuary annual survey and Gharial Conservation Alliance monitoring

species.habitat: Ponds, ditches and marsh in the lower Yangtze basin of Anhui and Zhejiang — now largely in reserves.
species.note: One of only two alligator species, and by far the rarer. It hibernates in burrows through cold Chinese winters. Fewer than a hundred mature animals survive in the wild, in fragments of farmland ditch, though captive numbers run to many thousands and releases are underway.
threats: Near-total conversion of its wetland habitat to rice paddy
Killing as a perceived threat to fish ponds

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Slow-moving freshwater — marsh, oxbow lake and forest stream, chiefly in Cambodia's Cardamom Mountains.
species.note: Declared effectively extinct in the wild in the 1990s, then rediscovered in the Cardamoms in 2000. Fewer than a thousand mature animals remain, while hundreds of thousands of hybrids live on commercial farms — which makes finding genetically pure wild stock its own conservation problem.
threats: Collection of eggs and young for crocodile farms

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Crocodile Specialist Group; Cambodian Cardamom Mountains surveys

species.habitat: Freshwater marsh, small lakes and creeks on Luzon and Mindanao.
species.note: A small, heavily armoured freshwater crocodile found nowhere else. Around a hundred adults remain in the wild. Community sanctuaries in northern Luzon, where villagers agreed to protect nesting creeks, hold the most successful population.
threats: Killing out of fear and for skins
Dynamite and electrofishing in its creeks

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Crocodile Specialist Group; Mabuwaya Foundation Luzon monitoring

species.habitat: Savanna, monsoon forest and coastal scrub on Komodo, Rinca, Flores and two smaller islands.
species.note: The largest lizard alive, up to three metres and 90 kg, with venom glands in the lower jaw that prevent a bitten animal's blood from clotting. Uplisted to Endangered in 2021 because sea-level rise is projected to remove a third of its low-lying habitat.
threats: Loss of deer prey to poaching
Tourism pressure on a very small range

pop.basis: Komodo National Park monitoring; total population including juveniles near 3,458

species.habitat: Large lowland rivers and lakes of the lower Yangtze and the Red River basin.
species.note: One of the largest freshwater turtles in the world and, by most counts, the rarest. Only two or three are known: a male in China's Suzhou Zoo, one animal in Xuan Khanh lake near Hanoi, and possibly another in Dong Mo lake, where the last known female was found dead in April 2023.
threats: Historic hunting for meat and shell

pop.basis: Asian Turtle Program field surveys, as reported by Mongabay

species.habitat: Cold, fast, rocky mountain streams in the Yangtze, Yellow and Pearl river basins.
species.note: The largest amphibian on Earth, reaching 1.8 m. It breathes through its skin, which is why it needs cold oxygen-rich water, and it calls with a sound uncannily like a human infant. Genetic work has since shown it to be several species, all of them in trouble.
threats: Harvesting for the luxury food trade
Farm escapes swamping wild populations with the wrong genetic lineage

pop.label: Wild populations are now vanishingly rare; surveys of 97 sites across China found almost no wild-origin animals.

species.habitat: The main channel of the Mekong and its deep dry-season pools, from Yunnan to the Tonle Sap.
species.note: One of the largest freshwater fish in the world — three metres, 300 kg — and toothless as an adult, grazing algae from rocks. It migrates hundreds of kilometres upstream to spawn, which dams make impossible.

pop.label: No population estimate; catch records indicate a decline of more than 80% over three generations.

species.habitat: The Yangtze River and adjacent East China Sea; spawns far upstream on gravel beds.
species.note: A living fossil that has been in the Yangtze for over 140 million years and can weigh half a tonne. The Gezhouba Dam cut it off from its spawning grounds in 1981. No natural spawning has been detected in the wild since 2017, and the species now persists mainly through hatchery releases.
threats: Dams blocking access to spawning gravel

pop.label: No confirmed natural spawning since 2017; the wild population is maintained by hatchery release.

species.habitat: Dense old-growth and secondary subtropical forest on Amami Ōshima and Tokunoshima, southern Japan.
species.note: A living fossil — a dark, short-eared, small-eyed rabbit whose lineage separated from all other rabbits millions of years ago. It digs burrows, is active only at night, and produces one or two young a year. Mongoose eradication on Amami has allowed a genuine recovery.
threats: Predation by introduced mongooses, now eradicated from Amami

pop.basis: Japanese Ministry of the Environment island surveys following mongoose eradication

species.habitat: Mediterranean scrub and open cork-oak woodland (dehesa) in Andalusia, Castilla-La Mancha and the Portuguese Guadiana.
species.note: In 2002 there were 94 animals in two isolated populations and it was the most endangered cat in the world. Captive breeding, rabbit restoration and 400 km of wildlife-crossing infrastructure took it past 2,000, and in 2024 the IUCN moved it from Endangered to Vulnerable — the largest recovery yet recorded for a wild cat.
threats: Collapse of its almost exclusive prey, the European rabbit, from viral disease
Road collisions, still the leading cause of death

pop.basis: Spain-Portugal coordinated annual census (LIFE Lynxconnect)

species.habitat: Densely vegetated banks of clean rivers and streams, and adjacent marsh.
species.note: One of Europe's most endangered mammals — it has lost more than 90% of its range and is now confined to a few river systems in Spain, France, Romania and Russia. Told from the American mink by white on both lips rather than just the lower.
threats: Displacement by introduced American mink, which is larger and outcompetes it

pop.label: Fewer than 30,000 in total and falling; the western populations are each under a few hundred animals.

species.habitat: Mixed deciduous woodland with open glades — chiefly Białowieża, the Carpathians and reintroduction sites west of them.
species.note: Europe's largest land mammal, extinct in the wild by 1927. Every animal alive descends from twelve captive founders. Reintroduction from studbook stock has taken it past 6,800 free-ranging animals and earned a downlisting from Vulnerable to Near Threatened in 2020.
threats: A gene pool descended from twelve founders

pop.basis: European Bison Pedigree Book; free-ranging and semi-free herds

species.habitat: Lake Saimaa in south-eastern Finland — a single freshwater lake, and nowhere else on Earth.
species.note: Stranded when the land lifted after the ice sheets melted, it has been landlocked for about 9,500 years. It pups in snowdrifts against the lakeshore, so mild winters are an existential problem: volunteers now shovel artificial drifts each February.
threats: Warm winters leaving too little snow for birth lairs
Drowning in gillnets, especially of pups
