pop.basis: Metsähallitus Parks & Wildlife Finland annual lair and moult counts

species.habitat: Deep loess and loam soils under cereal fields and steppe grassland across central and eastern Europe.
species.note: Within living memory this was an agricultural pest trapped by the million for its fur. It is now Critically Endangered — litter sizes have fallen from around twenty young a year to five or six, and no one is entirely sure why. Monoculture, light pollution and diet are all implicated.
threats: Collapse in reproductive rate under industrial monoculture
Loss of crop diversity and of overwinter cover

pop.label: No European total; national populations have fallen by more than 75% and several are near local extinction.

species.habitat: Rugged montane forest of the Mavrovo, Munella and Shebenik ranges in the western Balkans.
species.note: The most threatened lynx population in Europe, and possibly a distinct subspecies. Its 2015 assessment estimated fewer than forty mature animals, in the mountains where Albania, North Macedonia and Kosovo meet.
threats: A population too small for genetic health

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Cold, fast, clean mountain streams in the Pyrenees, Cantabrian range and northern Portugal.
species.note: A semi-aquatic mole with a flexible trunk-like snout, webbed hind feet and a rudder of a tail. It hunts insect larvae underwater by touch. It is disappearing from the southern half of its range, and in many rivers no one noticed until it had already gone.
threats: Water abstraction and small hydropower schemes

pop.label: No population estimate; the species has vanished from an estimated 60% of its historical Iberian range.

species.habitat: Beech forest and mountain pasture of the Abruzzo, Lazio and Molise National Park in the central Apennines.
species.note: Around sixty bears, isolated from all other brown bears for perhaps 400 years and now genetically distinct. They are unusually placid and largely vegetarian. A single bad year — poisoning, a road, an outbreak — could take a meaningful share of the population.

pop.basis: Parco Nazionale d'Abruzzo genetic and camera-trap monitoring

statusSource.text: Listed as Critically Endangered in the Italian Red List of vertebrates compiled by IUCN's Italian Committee.
statusSource.iucnNote: the IUCN Red List assesses the brown bear as a whole, as Least Concern

species.habitat: Cork-oak and holm-oak dehesa and Mediterranean scrub of central and southern Iberia.
species.note: Dark brown with brilliant white shoulder flashes, and dependent on rabbits in the same way the Iberian lynx is. Reduced to about 50 pairs in the 1960s, it has recovered past 800 breeding pairs through nest guarding, supplementary feeding and the retro-fitting of thousands of power pylons.

pop.basis: Spanish national census coordinated by MITECO and SEO/BirdLife

species.habitat: High mountain cliffs and alpine pasture, from the Pyrenees to the Himalaya and the Drakensberg.
species.note: The only vertebrate whose diet is mostly bone. It drops large ones from height onto rock slabs to shatter them, and its stomach acid dissolves the fragments. It bathes in iron-rich mud to stain its white breast rust-orange, apparently as a signal of status.
threats: Historic persecution that removed it from the Alps entirely
Collisions with power lines and wind turbines

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Breeds only on cliffs and islets of the Balearic Islands; disperses into the Bay of Biscay after breeding.
species.note: Europe's most endangered seabird. It breeds only in the Balearic Islands, and modelling suggests a mean time to extinction of decades rather than centuries unless bycatch and rat predation are stopped.
threats: Bycatch on longlines and in trawls
Rats and cats at breeding colonies

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Six high ledges in the central massif of Madeira, above 1,600 m — the entire breeding range.
species.note: Europe's rarest breeding seabird, known only from bones until a colony was found in 1969. Around 160 mature birds nest in burrows on ledges reachable only by rope. A 2010 wildfire killed two-thirds of that year's chicks.
threats: Predation by introduced rats and cats
A world population of a few hundred birds

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Open steppe, cereal plain and fallow grassland across Iberia, Central Europe and the Asian steppe.
species.note: The heaviest bird capable of flight — big males exceed 16 kg. In spring they invert their plumage into a mass of white feathers and vibrate, a display visible across kilometres of flat ground. Iberia holds about 70% of the world's population.
threats: Agricultural intensification and loss of fallow

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Open sedge fen — shallow, permanently wet, unwooded mire; winters in West African floodplains.
species.note: The only globally threatened migratory songbird in mainland Europe, tied to fen mire that has been drained almost everywhere. Belarus and Ukraine hold most of what is left. Males sing from sedge tussocks and take no part in raising the young.
threats: Drainage of sedge fen for peat and agriculture
Succession to scrub where mowing has stopped
Loss of West African wintering marshes

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Native laurel forest on the eastern tip of São Miguel, Azores — around 6,000 hectares in total.
species.note: Confined to one corner of one island. It was down to about 40 pairs in the 1970s. Removal of invasive Clethra and Australian cheesewood, and replanting of native laurel, has taken it past 1,000 birds — a recovery achieved almost entirely with a chainsaw and a nursery.
threats: Invasive plants replacing the native laurel it feeds in

pop.basis: SPEA (BirdLife Portugal) annual territory mapping, São Miguel

species.habitat: Rivers, lakes and estuaries across Europe and North Africa; spawns, so far as anyone knows, in the Sargasso Sea.
species.note: Every European eel is born in the middle of the Atlantic, drifts for a year or more as a transparent leaf, enters fresh water as a glass eel, lives up to twenty years, then swims 5,000 km back to spawn and die. Recruitment of young eels is down more than 90% since the 1980s.
threats: Barriers — weirs, dams and turbines — blocking migration
Glass eel trafficking, one of Europe's largest wildlife crimes
Parasites and pollutants carried in body fat
Changes in ocean currents affecting larval drift

pop.label: Recruitment of glass eels to European rivers is under 10% of 1980s levels and, in the North Sea, under 2%.

species.habitat: The Caspian and Black Seas, spawning far up the Volga, Ural and Danube.
species.note: Among the largest bony fish ever recorded — historical records describe animals over seven metres and a tonne — and the source of beluga caviar. Females do not spawn until fifteen or twenty years old, which is why a fishery can empty a river before anyone notices.
threats: Overfishing for caviar, legal and illegal
Dams blocking every major spawning river
Pollution in the Caspian and Black Sea catchments

pop.label: Natural reproduction has effectively ceased in most rivers; the Caspian population is maintained largely by hatchery release.

species.habitat: Sandy and muddy seabed from the shallows to 150 m; once common across the whole north-east Atlantic and Mediterranean.
species.note: A flattened, ambush-hunting shark that buries itself in sand and waits. Once abundant enough to be a nuisance in trawl nets, it has been eliminated from most of its range. The Canary Islands are now its global stronghold.
threats: Bottom trawling, which catches it incidentally wherever it occurs
Loss of shallow sandy nursery habitat

pop.label: Extirpated from most of the North Sea and much of the Mediterranean; the Canary Islands hold the only known stronghold.

species.habitat: Clean, cool, fast-flowing rivers with stable gravel beds and a healthy salmon or trout population.
species.note: It can live for more than 130 years, and its larvae must spend months attached to the gills of a salmon or trout to survive. Many European rivers now hold only elderly mussels — populations that look present but have not reproduced in decades.
threats: Silt from farming and forestry smothering gravel beds
Loss of salmon and trout hosts

pop.label: Europe has lost an estimated 90% of its pearl mussels; most surviving beds contain no juveniles at all.

species.habitat: Seven cold, shaded headwater streams in the Montseny massif, Catalonia — a range of a few square kilometres.
species.note: Described only in 2005, and the most endangered amphibian in Europe. It never leaves the water, lives among mossy stones in streams that stay under 15 °C, and the whole species could fit in a large aquarium.
threats: Drying of headwater streams under a warming, drier climate
Water abstraction for springs and farms
A total range of a few square kilometres

pop.basis: Diputació de Barcelona and IUCN assessment; capture-mark-recapture across the seven streams

species.habitat: Flooded limestone cave systems of the Dinaric karst, in total darkness.
species.note: A blind, unpigmented salamander that never leaves the larval form, can live over a century, and has been recorded going ten years without food. Slovenian villagers once believed they were baby dragons washed out of the rock by floods.
threats: Pollution of karst groundwater by farming and sewage
Extremely slow reproduction — a female may breed once a decade

pop.label: Population unknown and effectively uncountable; it is assessed on the basis of habitat quality and range decline.

species.habitat: Fast ice attached to the Antarctic coast — the only bird that breeds through the Antarctic winter.
species.note: Males incubate a single egg on their feet for over two months in -40 °C darkness, eating nothing, huddled in colonies that rotate so no bird stays on the windward edge. The species needs stable fast ice from April to December; in 2022 four colonies in the Bellingshausen Sea lost every chick when the ice broke up early.
threats: Loss of stable fast ice as the Southern Ocean warms
Projected loss of most colonies within this century under current emissions

pop.basis: Satellite survey of all known colonies (British Antarctic Survey); listed as Threatened under the US ESA in 2022

species.habitat: Open Southern Ocean, feeding along the Antarctic convergence in summer.
species.note: The largest animal that has ever lived — up to 33 m and 190 tonnes. Whaling removed roughly 99.7% of them: from about 239,000 before exploitation to a few hundred by 1973. Numbers are rising, but from a base so low that the subspecies remains Critically Endangered.
threats: A population still under 1% of its pre-whaling size

pop.basis: IWC Southern Ocean circumpolar surveys and IUCN assessment

species.habitat: Deep open ocean in all major basins, moving to polar feeding grounds in summer.
species.note: The third-largest whale and the fastest — it can hold 50 km/h in short bursts. Whalers turned to it after blue and fin whales were exhausted, taking more than 300,000 in the Southern Hemisphere alone during the twentieth century.
threats: Historic industrial whaling from which it has not recovered

pop.basis: IUCN Red List global assessment collating regional surveys

species.habitat: Deep water in every ocean; the Mediterranean holds a resident subpopulation of its own.
species.note: The second-largest animal on Earth, asymmetrically coloured — white on the right side of the jaw, dark on the left — which is thought to help it herd fish while circling. Its 20 Hz pulses carry for hundreds of kilometres.
threats: Ship strikes, the leading cause of death in busy seas

pop.basis: IUCN Red List global assessment; the Mediterranean subpopulation is separately Endangered

species.habitat: The open Southern Ocean; breeds on subantarctic islands including South Georgia, Crozet and Macquarie.
species.note: The largest wingspan of any living bird, up to 3.5 m, and a body built to travel — it can circle Antarctica in 46 days and glide for hours without a wingbeat. Pairs bond for life and raise one chick every two years.
threats: Longline and trawl fishery bycatch, chiefly of adults
Introduced mice attacking chicks on breeding islands

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Subantarctic islands and the Antarctic Peninsula; forages far offshore for krill and lanternfish.
species.note: The most numerous penguin in the world and still Vulnerable — its population has fallen by more than half since the 1970s. Named by 18th-century sailors after the flamboyant 'macaroni' fashion for its drooping orange crest.
threats: Reduction in krill availability as the Southern Ocean warms
Introduced predators at some breeding sites

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International
pop.label: The assessment counts about 6.3 million breeding pairs in some 258 colonies.

species.habitat: Rocky subantarctic coasts and tussock slopes, chiefly the Falklands, Tierra del Fuego and the Indian Ocean islands.
species.note: A small penguin with a spiked yellow eyebrow crest that hops up cliffs rather than climbing them. The Falkland population alone fell from more than 1.5 million pairs in the 1930s to a fraction of that, largely because of changes in the food supply.
threats: Shifts in prey distribution driven by ocean warming
Introduced rats and cats at some sites

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Shallow, turbid water at the very top of the Gulf of California — a range smaller than metropolitan Los Angeles.
species.note: The smallest porpoise on Earth and the most endangered marine mammal. Dark rings around the eyes and lips give it a permanently startled expression. It has never been held alive in captivity, and every animal that dies now is a measurable fraction of the species.
threats: Drowning in gillnets set illegally for totoaba, whose swim bladder is trafficked to China
A range of a few hundred square kilometres
Enforcement failure in the Upper Gulf refuge

pop.basis: Acoustic and visual survey of the Zero Tolerance Area, Upper Gulf of California

species.habitat: Coastal and shelf waters from Florida's calving grounds to the Gulf of St Lawrence.
species.note: Named because whalers considered it the 'right' whale to kill: slow, coastal, and it floats when dead. Around 370 remain, every one individually known from the callosity pattern on its head. No calf has been born to most females in years, because entanglement injuries suppress reproduction.
threats: Entanglement in fixed fishing gear, which injures or kills most adults at some point
Shift of feeding grounds north into unprotected waters

pop.basis: North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium photo-identification catalogue, New England Aquarium

species.habitat: A single strip of the north-eastern Gulf of Mexico along the continental shelf break off Florida.
species.note: Recognised as a distinct species only in 2021, and immediately one of the rarest whales in the world — roughly fifty animals, all in one body of water crossed constantly by shipping and oil infrastructure.
threats: Vessel strikes in one of the world's busiest shipping regions
Oil spills and seismic survey noise
A population of about fifty animals with no refuge

pop.basis: NOAA Fisheries Gulf of Mexico line-transect surveys

species.habitat: Chaparral, oak savanna and coastal cliffs of California, Arizona, Utah and Baja California.
species.note: The largest land bird in North America, with a three-metre wingspan. In 1987 the last 22 were taken into captivity — the entire species. Every condor alive descends from 14 of them. Around 350 now fly free, and almost all of them are periodically recaptured to be treated for lead poisoning.
threats: Lead poisoning from ammunition fragments in carcasses
A gene pool descended from 14 founders

pop.basis: US Fish and Wildlife Service annual population status report; roughly 344 of these fly free

species.habitat: Breeds in the muskeg of Wood Buffalo National Park, Canada; winters on the Texas coast at Aransas.
species.note: North America's tallest bird at over 1.5 m. It fell to fifteen birds in 1941 — a single flock. The wild Aransas-Wood Buffalo population is now over 500, still using the same 4,000 km migration route their ancestors flew, learned by each generation from the last.
threats: Loss of coastal wintering marsh to sea level and freshwater diversion

pop.basis: US Fish and Wildlife Service and Canadian Wildlife Service joint status report, wild and captive combined

species.habitat: Pine savanna, farmland and coastal marsh of the Albemarle Peninsula, eastern North Carolina.
species.note: Pronounced extinct in the wild in 1980; fourteen animals were captured to found a breeding programme and released back in 1987. The wild population peaked near 130 and has since fallen to under two dozen. Most known deaths are gunshots.
threats: Gunshot mortality, the leading known cause of death
A wild population in the low double digits

pop.basis: US Fish and Wildlife Service Red Wolf Recovery Program counts; around 270 more are held in captivity

species.habitat: Ponderosa pine and pinyon-juniper woodland of Arizona, New Mexico and the Sierra Madre Occidental.
species.note: The smallest and most genetically distinct grey wolf in North America. Extinct in the wild by 1980; seven founders were used to rebuild it. The US wild population passed 250 in 2023, and cross-fostering of captive pups into wild dens is used to widen the gene pool.
threats: A founder population of seven animals

pop.basis: Interagency Field Team annual Mexican wolf count, Arizona and New Mexico

statusSource.text: Listed as Endangered under the US Endangered Species Act.
statusSource.iucnNote: the IUCN Red List assesses the grey wolf as a whole

species.habitat: Shortgrass and mixed-grass prairie, entirely dependent on prairie dog colonies for food and burrows.
species.note: Declared extinct twice. In 1981 a ranch dog in Wyoming brought a dead one home, leading to the discovery of the last colony; eighteen animals were taken in and seven bred. North America's most endangered mammal now numbers around 300 in the wild, all requiring plague vaccination.
threats: Sylvatic plague, which kills both ferrets and their prairie dog prey
Historic eradication of prairie dogs across 95% of the range

pop.basis: US Fish and Wildlife Service Black-footed Ferret Recovery Program reintroduction site counts

species.habitat: Cypress swamp, hardwood hammock and pine flatwood in south-west Florida, south of the Caloosahatchee.
species.note: The last puma population east of the Mississippi. By 1995 inbreeding had produced kinked tails, heart defects and undescended testicles; eight Texas females were released to restore genetic variation, and it worked. Vehicle strikes now kill more panthers than anything else.
threats: Habitat loss to development in south Florida

pop.basis: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission population estimate

statusSource.text: Listed as Endangered under the US Endangered Species Act since 1967.
statusSource.iucnNote: the IUCN Red List assesses the puma as a whole, as Least Concern

species.habitat: Beaches, atolls and shallow reefs of the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, plus a growing group in the main islands.
species.note: One of the rarest seals on Earth and one of only two tropical seal species left — the third, the Caribbean monk seal, was declared extinct in 2008. Around 1,600 remain, and the population has grown slowly for over a decade.
threats: Predation on pups by Galapagos sharks at French Frigate Shoals
Loss of pupping beaches to sea-level rise
Disease, including toxoplasmosis from cat faeces in runoff

pop.basis: NOAA Fisheries Hawaiian Monk Seal Research Program range-wide count

species.habitat: Kelp forest and rocky nearshore water of the North Pacific rim.
species.note: It has no blubber — instead, the densest fur of any animal, up to a million hairs per square inch, which is exactly why the fur trade reduced it from around 300,000 to perhaps 2,000 animals by 1911. By eating urchins it keeps kelp forests standing, which makes it the textbook keystone species.
threats: Oil spills, which destroy the insulating properties of the fur
Killer whale predation in the Aleutians

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment collating US, Canadian and Russian survey data

species.habitat: Sea ice over the continental shelves of the Arctic Ocean, where seals are reachable.
species.note: It is classified as a marine mammal because it depends entirely on sea ice as a hunting platform. Hudson Bay bears now fast on land for around a month longer than they did forty years ago, and body condition and cub survival have fallen in step.
threats: Loss of sea ice, reducing access to seals

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Polar Bear Specialist Group global assessment across 19 subpopulations

species.habitat: Subalpine meadows and avalanche chutes between 900 and 1,500 m on Vancouver Island, British Columbia.
species.note: Canada's most endangered mammal, and found on one island. Numbers fell to about thirty animals in 2003. Captive breeding and release have taken it back over 200, though every colony is still monitored individually.
threats: Predation by wolves, cougars and eagles on a tiny population
Clear-cut logging creating ecological traps that draw marmots to unsuitable slopes

pop.basis: Marmot Recovery Foundation annual census, Vancouver Island

species.habitat: High-elevation ʻōhiʻa and koa–ʻōhiʻa forest on Kauaʻi; its last stronghold was the Alakaʻi, at 1,000–1,600 m.
species.note: A honeycreeper found only on Kauaʻi, estimated at 6,832 birds in 1968–73 and 468 in 2012. Avian malaria, spread by introduced mosquitoes that now survive higher up the mountains as temperatures rise, then took hold across its range. By the end of 2024 Hawaiʻi's Department of Land and Natural Resources considered it functionally extinct in the wild, and the last known wild bird, a female named Pakele, was last seen on 29 August 2025. The species survives in a conservation breeding flock run by San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance.
threats: Avian malaria and pox spread by introduced mosquitoes
Warming that lets mosquitoes survive at higher elevations
Hurricanes that push birds downslope into malarial forest
Forest degradation by feral pigs and invasive plants

pop.basis: Kauaʻi Forest Bird Recovery Project monitoring
pop.label: The last known wild bird was last seen on 29 August 2025. The IUCN's 2018 estimate of 150–610 mature individuals predates the collapse.

species.habitat: Wet montane ʻōhiʻa and koa forest on the windward slope of Haleakalā, Maui.
species.note: The Maui parrotbill — a stocky honeycreeper with a heavy hooked bill it uses to tear open branches for beetle larvae, like a small parrot with a crowbar. Around 150 remain, on one mountain slope.
threats: Loss of native forest to feral pigs and cattle
A single population of roughly 150 birds

pop.basis: Maui Forest Bird Recovery Project distance-sampling surveys

species.habitat: Dry māmane forest on the upper western slope of Mauna Kea, Hawaiʻi Island.
species.note: Golden-headed, grey-backed, and dependent on the seed pods of a single tree — the māmane — which it opens with a heavy finch bill. Feral sheep and goats browsed the māmane forest to a fraction of its extent, and the bird's range shrank with it.
threats: Browsing of māmane by feral sheep and goats

pop.basis: US Geological Survey annual Palila abundance survey, Mauna Kea

species.habitat: The remaining canals and chinampa wetlands of Xochimilco, in the south of Mexico City.
species.note: It never metamorphoses — it becomes sexually mature while keeping its feathery larval gills — and it can regrow limbs, jaw, spinal cord and parts of its brain. Hundreds of thousands live in laboratories and aquariums worldwide; in the wild it is nearly gone from the single lake system it evolved in.
threats: Water pollution and sewage in the Xochimilco canals
Introduced carp and tilapia eating eggs and larvae
A wild range of a few square kilometres

pop.label: Density fell from roughly 6,000 per km² in 1998 to 36 per km² in 2014; the most recent surveys found almost none.

species.habitat: Zacatón bunchgrass under open pine forest on four volcanoes ringing Mexico City, between 2,800 and 4,250 m.
species.note: The second-smallest rabbit in the world, with tiny rounded ears and no visible tail. It lives only in dense bunchgrass on volcanic slopes, and it is one of very few rabbits that vocalises — a high whistle used as an alarm.
threats: Burning of zacatón grassland for pasture
Urban and agricultural expansion up the volcano slopes

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment; Sierra Chichinautzin and Ajusco transect counts

species.habitat: Lowland and montane rainforest, swamp and cloud forest from southern Mexico to northern Colombia.
species.note: The largest land mammal in Central America, and a walking seed disperser — it carries large seeds far from the trees that dropped them. Belize made it the national animal; the region has lost most of its population anyway.
threats: Fragmentation of forest by cattle ranching

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Tapir Specialist Group range-wide estimate

species.habitat: The Gulf of Mexico and north-west Atlantic; nests almost entirely on one beach at Rancho Nuevo, Tamaulipas.
species.note: The smallest and most endangered sea turtle. It nests by day in mass arrivals called arribadas — a 1947 film recorded 40,000 females on one beach in a single afternoon. By 1985 the annual total was 702 nests. Bi-national protection rebuilt it, then the recovery stalled.
threats: Egg poaching, now largely controlled at the main beach
Oil spills in the Gulf of Mexico
Dependence on essentially one nesting beach

pop.basis: Bi-national Kemp's Ridley Working Group nest counts, Rancho Nuevo

species.habitat: Dry limestone forest of the Hellshire Hills, southern Jamaica.
species.note: Believed extinct for four decades until a pig hunter's dog caught one in 1990. The Hellshire population — the only one — was down to a few dozen adults. Head-starting young in captivity until they are too large for mongooses to kill has taken it past 300.
threats: Predation of young by introduced Indian mongooses
Charcoal burning destroying dry limestone forest

pop.basis: Jamaican Iguana Recovery Group monitoring, Hellshire Hills

species.habitat: Lowland and mid-elevation broadleaf forest in the Dominican Republic; essentially confined to Los Haitises.
species.note: Endemic to Hispaniola and reduced to one core population. The main killer of chicks is a parasitic botfly; field teams treat nestlings individually. Assisted dispersal to new sites has begun to build a second population.
threats: Nestling parasitism by Philornis botfly larvae

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Pine forest and coppice with understorey palms on Andros Island, Bahamas.
species.note: Split as a full species in 2010 and confined to Andros — it disappeared from Abaco decades earlier. Its nests are built in the fronds of understorey thatch palm, a habitat only recently discovered by researchers.
threats: Lethal yellowing disease killing the coconut palms it nested in

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Freshwater swamp — the Zapata Swamp and the Lanier Swamp on Isla de la Juventud, and nowhere else.
species.note: The most terrestrial crocodilian, with strong legs, a short snout and a habit of leaping from the water. It has the smallest natural range of any crocodile, and hybridisation with American crocodiles is steadily eroding what is genetically distinct about it.
threats: A natural range confined to two swamps

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Forest streams of Panama between 335 and 1,315 m, including El Valle de Antón.
species.note: Made a national symbol of Panama by law in 2010, with 14 August as National Golden Frog Day. Chytridiomycosis reached El Valle de Antón in 2006, and no golden frog has been recorded in the wild since 2009. More than 1,000 adults live at over 50 institutions in the United States and Canada. In a trial reported in 2026, 100 captive-bred frogs spent 12 weeks in soft-release pens in Panama; about 70% died of the same disease, and many of the survivors were then released.

pop.unit: mature individuals known in the wild
pop.basis: IUCN SSC Amphibian Specialist Group assessment, which records no known wild location

species.habitat: Tallgrass prairie remnants, woodland edge and gardens in the upper Midwest and north-eastern United States.
species.note: Once one of the commonest bumblebees from Maine to the Dakotas, it has disappeared from an estimated 87% of its range in twenty years. In 2017 it became the first bumblebee listed under the US Endangered Species Act.
threats: Pathogen spillover from commercially reared bumblebees
Loss of prairie and continuous season-long flowering

pop.label: No population estimate; occupancy has fallen by roughly 87% and the range by about 90% since the late 1990s.

species.habitat: Breeds across North America on milkweed; overwinters in Mexican oyamel fir forest and coastal California groves.
species.note: The eastern population makes a 4,000 km migration that takes several generations to complete, navigating to fir groves none of them have ever seen. It was assessed as Endangered in 2022 and reassessed as Vulnerable in 2023 after the methodology was revised; the western population has separately fallen by more than 95%.
threats: Loss of milkweed from herbicide-tolerant crop systems
Degradation of the Mexican overwintering forest
Pesticide exposure across the breeding range

pop.label: Measured as forest area occupied rather than as individuals: the eastern overwintering colonies covered 0.9 ha in 2024, against a long-term average near 6 ha.

species.habitat: A single water-filled limestone cavern in the Amargosa Desert, Nevada — the smallest range of any vertebrate.
species.note: The entire species lives on and above one shallow rock shelf about the size of a dining table, in 33 °C water. It has been there for somewhere between a few thousand and tens of thousands of years. The count has run as low as 35 fish.
threats: A total habitat of one cavern shelf
Groundwater pumping lowering the water level
Earthquake-driven surges that scour the spawning shelf
Extreme vulnerability to any single event

pop.basis: National Park Service and US Fish and Wildlife Service biannual Devils Hole count

species.habitat: Shallow coastal water, estuaries and mangrove shoreline; young stay in mangrove nurseries for years.
species.note: A ray, not a shark, with a flattened rostrum edged in tooth-like scales that it swipes sideways through schools of fish. The saw catches in nets so reliably that the species was eliminated from most of its range. The United States now holds one of the last viable populations, in south-west Florida.
threats: Entanglement in gillnets and trawls, caused by the saw itself
Historic trade in rostra as curios

pop.label: Extirpated from an estimated 81% of its former range; the US population is stable and slowly expanding.

species.habitat: Shallow, high-energy reef crest of the Caribbean, from the surface to about 5 m.
species.note: The reef-builder that made Caribbean reef crests — broad, flattened branches like antlers, growing up to 10 cm a year. White band disease removed roughly 97% of it from the 1980s onward, and stony coral tissue loss disease has since arrived on top of that.
threats: White band disease and stony coral tissue loss disease
Physical damage from storms and anchoring

pop.label: Cover has fallen by roughly 97% across the Caribbean since 1980; recovery is limited by disease rather than by space.

species.habitat: Lowland Atlantic Forest fragments in Rio de Janeiro state, chiefly the São João river basin.
species.note: Brilliant orange, with a mane like a small lion, and down to about 200 animals in the early 1970s. Reintroduction, forest corridors and a landowner programme took it past 3,700 — then a yellow fever outbreak in 2018 killed roughly a third. Vaccination of wild tamarins has since begun.
threats: Yellow fever outbreaks in a small population
Fragmentation of Atlantic Forest by pasture and roads
Illegal capture for the pet trade
Only about 2% of the original forest remains

pop.basis: Associação Mico-Leão-Dourado census following the 2018 yellow fever outbreak

species.habitat: Dry and humid tropical forest of north-western Colombia, between the Atrato and Magdalena rivers.
species.note: A tamarin the weight of a bag of sugar with a shock of white hair swept back like a punk crest. Thousands were exported for biomedical research in the 1960s and 70s. Around 7,400 remain in a forest that has been reduced to under 5% of its original extent.
threats: Loss of dry tropical forest to cattle and charcoal
Capture for the local pet trade

pop.basis: Proyecto Tití range-wide population and habitat modelling

species.habitat: Montane Atlantic Forest fragments in Minas Gerais, Espírito Santo and Bahia.
species.note: The largest primate in the Americas, and among the most peaceable of all monkeys — males do not fight over females, and groups embrace to settle tension. Around 1,000 remain in a dozen forest fragments, the largest holding perhaps 350.
threats: Fragmentation of Atlantic Forest into isolated patches

pop.basis: Muriqui Instituto de Biodiversidade fragment censuses

species.habitat: Cloud forest between 1,500 and 2,700 m on the eastern slope of the Peruvian Andes.
species.note: Endemic to a narrow band of Peruvian cloud forest, thick-furred against the cold, with a yellow patch under the tail tip. Known from a single specimen for over a century before a live population was found in 1974.
threats: Road building opening cloud forest to settlement
Conversion to coffee and cattle pasture

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group; Yambrasbamba and Río Nieva survey estimates

species.habitat: Lowland and montane forest of the Magdalena and Catatumbo valleys of Colombia and north-western Venezuela.
species.note: One of the twenty-five most endangered primates in the world, with pale blue eyes unusual among New World monkeys. Its forest sits over Colombia's oil and cattle heartland and has been almost entirely cleared.
threats: Near-total clearance of the Magdalena valley forest
Capture of infants for the pet trade

pop.label: No population estimate; the assessment records a decline exceeding 80% over three generations.

species.habitat: Seasonally flooded palm savanna of the Llanos de Moxos in Beni department, Bolivia.
species.note: Endemic to one Bolivian floodplain and unknown in the wild until 1992. It nests only in the hollows of dead motacú palms, which cattle ranchers clear — so the recovery has been built on nest boxes, several hundred of them.
threats: Historic trapping for the pet trade
Loss of dead palms used for nesting
A world population of a few hundred

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Sandstone cliffs and licuri palm stands in the Caatinga of northern Bahia, Brazil.
species.note: Known only from trade birds until its wild colony was found in 1978 — about sixty birds on two sandstone cliffs. Cliff guarding, licuri palm planting and compensation to maize farmers have taken it past 1,700 and earned two successive downlistings.
threats: Loss of licuri palm, its almost exclusive food

pop.basis: Brazilian ICMBio and Fundação Biodiversitas coordinated cliff roost counts

species.habitat: Pantanal wetland, Cerrado gallery forest and Amazonian palm savanna.
species.note: The largest flying parrot in the world at a metre long, cobalt blue with a bare yellow eye-ring. A bill strong enough to crack a palm nut a person cannot open with a hammer. Trapping took perhaps 10,000 birds in the 1980s; nest boxes and ranch partnerships in the Pantanal have since roughly doubled the population.
threats: Historic trapping for the pet trade
Conversion of Cerrado to soy and cattle

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Remote basaltic plateau lakes of Santa Cruz province, Patagonia; winters on two Atlantic estuaries.
species.note: Discovered only in 1974. It builds floating nests on mats of aquatic milfoil in high, windswept lakes, and the population has fallen by around 80% since then. Introduced American mink and kelp gulls take eggs and chicks; volunteers now camp beside colonies all summer to guard them.
threats: Lakes drying under a warming, drier Patagonian climate

pop.basis: Aves Argentinas Proyecto Macá Tobiano plateau-wide lake surveys

species.habitat: Fast, exceptionally clear rivers in the Cerrado, chiefly the Serra da Canastra region of Minas Gerais.
species.note: One of the rarest waterfowl in the world, with fewer than 250 mature birds. It needs water clear enough to hunt fish by sight, so any siltation of a river removes it permanently. Pairs hold long stretches of river and stay together year-round.
threats: Siltation from agriculture, mining and road building

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Humid forest along spring-fed streams at the foot of the Araripe plateau, Ceará, Brazil — about 30 km².
species.note: Described in 1998, and confined to a strip of moist forest at the base of one escarpment where springs emerge. Males are white with a scarlet crown and crest; females are olive. Fewer than 700 mature birds remain.
threats: Diversion of springs for water parks and irrigation
Clearance of streamside forest for banana and sugarcane
A total range of about 30 km²

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Lake Junín, a high Andean lake at 4,100 m in central Peru — its entire world range.
species.note: Flightless, and found on one lake. Mine tailings from the Cerro de Pasco district have contaminated the lake for a century, and water level is manipulated for hydropower, which strands nests. Only a few hundred birds remain.
threats: Heavy metal contamination from mine drainage
Water level manipulation for hydroelectricity stranding nests
A single lake as its entire range

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: The Andes from Colombia to Tierra del Fuego, and Pacific coastal cliffs where cold currents produce updraughts.
species.note: The largest flying bird in the world by combined wingspan and weight. A tracking study found one bird flew 172 km without a single wingbeat. It lays one egg every two or three years, so poisoning of a few adults can empty a valley for a generation.
threats: Poisoned bait set for pumas and foxes
Lead poisoning from ammunition in carcasses

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Arid scrub and cactus woodland on Española, the southernmost island of the Galápagos.
species.note: In 1960 fourteen animals were left, so scattered across the island that they had not met in years. All were taken into captivity, joined by a male repatriated from San Diego Zoo, and the fifteen produced more than 2,000 offspring. Goat eradication let them be released. The population is now self-sustaining.
threats: A gene pool descended from fifteen animals

pop.basis: Galápagos National Park Directorate and Charles Darwin Foundation island monitoring

species.habitat: Rocky lava shorelines of Fernandina and western Isabela, cooled by the Cromwell upwelling.
species.note: The one penguin whose range reaches north of the equator, kept alive by a cold current in the tropics. It pants and holds its flippers out to shed heat. Strong El Niño events cut off the upwelling, and in 1982-83 roughly three-quarters of the population starved.
threats: El Niño events removing the food supply
Introduced rats and cats at nest sites

pop.basis: Charles Darwin Foundation annual Galápagos penguin and cormorant census

species.habitat: Two tiny satellite islets — Champion and Gardner-by-Floreana — off Floreana in the Galápagos.
species.note: The bird Darwin collected on Floreana in 1835, and the specimen that first made him doubt the fixity of species. It was extinct on Floreana itself within fifty years. Around 500 survive on two islets, together smaller than a large farm.
threats: Extinction on the main island from rats, cats and goats
A total range of two islets under 10 hectares each
Vulnerability to a single introduction event

pop.basis: Charles Darwin Foundation islet censuses

species.habitat: Slow rivers, oxbow lakes and flooded forest of the Amazon, Orinoco and Pantanal basins.
species.note: Up to 1.8 m long — the longest otter in the world. Family groups are noisy and cooperative, and each animal has a unique white throat pattern that works as a name badge. The fur trade took an estimated 20,000 skins a year in the 1960s.
threats: Mercury contamination from artisanal gold mining
Habitat loss from dams and deforestation
Historic fur hunting from which many rivers never recovered

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment collating basin-level survey data

species.habitat: The Amazon and Orinoco basins, including flooded forest that it swims through between the trunks.
species.note: Pink, flexible-necked, and able to turn its head 90 degrees to hunt among submerged branches. Its eyes work, unlike the Ganges dolphin's, but it hunts mainly by sonar in black water. Numbers at long-studied sites have been halving roughly every decade.
threats: Deliberate killing for use as bait in the piracatinga fishery
Mercury from gold mining accumulating up the food chain

pop.label: No basin-wide total; monitored populations have declined by about 50% every ten years since the mid-1990s.

species.habitat: Cloud forest, páramo and dry forest along the Andes from Venezuela to Bolivia.
species.note: South America's only bear, and the last surviving short-faced bear. Cream markings around the eyes are unique to each animal. It spends much of its life in trees, building platforms of broken branches to feed from and sleep on.
threats: Fragmentation of Andean forest by agriculture
Killing after crop and livestock damage
Poaching for gall bladders and paws

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Steep Andean forest, scree and alpine meadow of southern Chile and Argentine Patagonia.
species.note: Chile's national animal, appearing on the coat of arms, and reduced to under 1,500 across a range once ten times as large. Short-legged and heavy-bodied for climbing, it is unusually approachable — which historically made it very easy to shoot.
threats: Fragmentation into more than 100 tiny subpopulations

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Deer Specialist Group binational estimate

species.habitat: High Andean rocky steppe and puna above 3,000 m, and the Patagonian steppe in Argentina.
species.note: One of the least-known cats in the world — ash-grey with rust blotches and a thick banded tail nearly as long as its body. It was not photographed alive in the wild until 1998. Its 2024 assessment estimated about 2,200 mature animals.
threats: Killing for traditional ceremonial use and by herding dogs
Decline of its main prey, the mountain viscacha

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Temperate Valdivian rainforest on Chiloé Island, the Nahuelbuta range and a few coastal patches.
species.note: Collected by Darwin on Chiloé in 1834 — he thought it a variety of another fox; it turned out to be a distinct species restricted to Chilean rainforest. Small, dark and short-legged, with around a thousand animals left in three separated populations.
threats: Attacks and disease from domestic and feral dogs

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Canid Specialist Group; Chiloé and Nahuelbuta population estimates

species.habitat: Rainforest, wetland, dry forest and scrub from the south-western United States to northern Argentina.
species.note: The largest cat in the Americas and the one with the strongest bite relative to size — it kills by piercing the skull rather than the throat. Globally Near Threatened, but that hides the detail: it has been lost from half its historical range, and several regional populations are Critically Endangered.
threats: Habitat conversion for cattle and soy
Emerging trade in teeth and bones to Asian markets

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group range-wide estimate; most animals are in the Amazon

species.habitat: Cerrado grassland, scrub savanna and marsh edge of central South America.
species.note: Not a wolf and not a fox — the only member of its genus, built like a red fox on stilts, with legs long enough to see over tall grass. Roughly half its diet is a fruit, the lobeira or wolf apple, whose seeds germinate best after passing through it.
threats: Conversion of Cerrado to soy and sugarcane
Road collisions, the leading recorded cause of death

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Canid Specialist Group range-wide estimate

species.habitat: Cerrado, Pantanal and Amazonian forest with deep soils it can dig into.
species.note: Up to 50 kg, with the largest claw of any living animal relative to body size — a foreclaw longer than a human hand, used to open termite mounds. It is nocturnal and so rarely seen that its burrows are studied far more often than the animal itself. Its abandoned burrows shelter dozens of other species.
threats: Conversion of Cerrado and Pantanal to cropland
Very low reproductive rate — one young every few years

pop.label: No population estimate; assessed as declining by more than 30% over three generations and naturally very sparse.

species.habitat: Lake Titicaca and its satellite lakes, at 3,800 m in the Andes.
species.note: It breathes almost entirely through its skin, which hangs in loose folds to increase surface area in oxygen-poor water — the reason for its unkind nickname, the scrotum frog. It does bob up and down on the bottom to move water over those folds.
threats: Harvesting for 'frog juice' sold as a tonic
Pollution and sewage entering the lake

pop.label: No total estimate; mass mortality events have killed more than 10,000 frogs at a time in the Coata river.

species.habitat: Lowland rainforest on the Pacific slope of Cauca department, Colombia — a range of about 200 km².
species.note: The most poisonous animal known: one wild adult carries enough batrachotoxin to kill several people. It gets the toxin from its diet, so captive-bred animals are harmless. Emberá hunters wiped blowgun darts on its back — the origin of the name.
threats: Clearance of Chocó rainforest for coca, gold mining and logging

pop.label: No population estimate; restricted to a handful of localities within about 200 km².

species.habitat: Volcanic slopes and the Andean-Patagonian forest of south-central Chile and adjacent Argentina.
species.note: A conifer that has changed little in 200 million years, with stiff triangular leaves running right down the trunk — armour against browsing dinosaurs, so the story goes. Individuals live over a thousand years. Its seeds, piñones, are a staple food for Mapuche-Pehuenche communities.
threats: An undiagnosed dieback disease affecting mature trees

pop.label: No individual count; the assessment records a population reduction of more than 50% over three generations, with fire the dominant driver.

species.habitat: Predator-free islands such as Whenua Hou and Anchor Island, after extinction on the unfenced mainland.
species.note: The only parrot that cannot fly, the heaviest at up to 4 kg, and among the longest-lived birds. Males boom from a hollowed bowl in the earth on still nights, a sound that carries five kilometres but is nearly impossible to locate. Every living kākāpō has a name and a transmitter.
threats: Introduced stoats, rats and cats, which caused the mainland extinction
Breeding tied to rimu masting, which occurs every few years
A gene pool descended from about 50 birds

pop.basis: New Zealand Department of Conservation Kākāpō Recovery Programme; every bird is individually tracked

species.habitat: Alpine tussock grassland of the Murchison Mountains and a network of predator-free island sanctuaries.
species.note: Declared extinct in 1898 and rediscovered in 1948 in a remote Fiordland valley — one of the great rediscoveries in ornithology. A heavy, flightless, iridescent blue-green rail with a scarlet bill. The population has passed 500 and birds were returned to the mainland Greenstone valley in 2023.
threats: Competition with introduced red deer for tussock

pop.basis: Department of Conservation Takahē Recovery Programme annual count

species.habitat: Scrub forest on Mangere and Rangatira islands in the Chatham group, east of New Zealand.
species.note: In 1980 five birds remained, of which one female — 'Old Blue' — was still fertile. Every black robin alive is her descendant. Cross-fostering eggs to tomtits saved the species; the whole population passed 250 within two decades.
threats: A gene pool descended from a single breeding female
Inbreeding effects, including an inherited egg-laying defect

pop.basis: Department of Conservation Chatham Islands island censuses

species.habitat: Shallow inshore waters off the west coast of the North Island, New Zealand.
species.note: The world's rarest marine dolphin — around 54 animals over a year old. It is small enough to be mistaken for a seal, with a rounded dorsal fin like a Mickey Mouse ear. A single entanglement death per year is more than the population can absorb.
threats: Entanglement in set nets and trawls
Toxoplasmosis from cat faeces washed into the sea
Seabed mining and oil exploration proposals

pop.basis: New Zealand Department of Conservation and Fisheries NZ genetic mark-recapture survey

species.habitat: Coastal forest and scrub of south-eastern New Zealand, Stewart Island and the subantarctic Auckland Islands.
species.note: Hoiho — 'noise shouter' in te reo Māori. Unlike most penguins it nests alone, out of sight of other pairs, in coastal forest. The mainland population has fallen steeply and could be gone within decades; the subantarctic islands hold the bulk of what remains.

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Alpine and subalpine forest and scree of the South Island, up to 2,000 m.
species.note: The world's only alpine parrot, and one of the most inquisitive birds alive — it dismantles car windscreen wipers and solves multi-step puzzles. Olive-green with scarlet underwings. Persecuted as a sheep killer until 1970, when a bounty was still being paid.
threats: Lead poisoning from flashing and nails on old buildings
Predation by stoats and possums at ground nests
Human food conditioning around ski fields

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Beaches and coastal forest of the Auckland and Campbell Islands, with a small recolonising group on the mainland.
species.note: One of the rarest sea lions in the world. It once bred all around New Zealand and was reduced to the subantarctic; females have recently begun pupping on Otago beaches again, sometimes walking a kilometre inland through farmland to give birth in forest.
threats: Bycatch in the squid trawl fishery
Bacterial epidemics killing pups at the Auckland Islands
A breeding range concentrated on two island groups

pop.basis: Department of Conservation Auckland and Campbell Islands pup production counts

species.habitat: Deep sandy soils under semi-arid grassland at Epping Forest National Park, Queensland, plus two translocation sites.
species.note: One of the rarest large mammals on Earth. In the 1980s about 35 remained in a single Queensland park. A dingo-proof fence and careful management have taken it past 400, and two insurance colonies have been established.
threats: A single main population in one small park
Drought and competition with cattle for grass

pop.basis: Queensland Department of Environment and Science hair-sample census, Epping Forest

species.habitat: Dense long-unburnt heath at Two Peoples Bay, Western Australia, and two translocation sites.
species.note: Australia's most endangered mammal, believed extinct for over a century until rediscovered in 1994. It eats almost nothing but underground fungi — around 90% of its diet — which ties it to old heath that has not burnt in decades.
threats: Fire, which removes the truffle-bearing heath it depends on
A diet almost entirely of fungi

pop.basis: Western Australia Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions trapping census

species.habitat: Wandoo and jarrah eucalypt woodland with fallen hollow logs, south-western Western Australia.
species.note: A marsupial with no pouch and 50 teeth, more than any other Australian land mammal, which it barely uses — it eats up to 20,000 termites a day, taken with a long sticky tongue. It is strictly diurnal, unusual for an Australian marsupial, because termites are.
threats: Predation by introduced red foxes and feral cats
Loss of hollow logs used for shelter

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Dry sclerophyll forest, coastal scrub and farmland across Tasmania.
species.note: The largest surviving marsupial carnivore, with the strongest bite for its size of any living mammal. Since 1996 it has been ravaged by devil facial tumour disease — one of only a handful of transmissible cancers known in nature, passed on when the animals bite each other's faces.
threats: Devil facial tumour disease, which has killed roughly 80% of the population
A second, independently arisen transmissible tumour

pop.basis: Tasmanian Save the Tasmanian Devil Program statewide spotlighting surveys

species.habitat: Eucalypt forest and woodland along the eastern and southern coasts of Australia.
species.note: It eats leaves so low in energy and high in toxin that it sleeps up to 20 hours a day to digest them, and it has a specialised gut flora that joeys acquire by eating their mother's droppings. The 2019-20 bushfires killed or displaced an estimated 60,000 koalas in a single season.
threats: Clearing of eucalypt woodland for housing and agriculture
Chlamydia infection causing blindness and infertility

pop.label: No agreed national total; the eastern populations were uplisted to Endangered under Australian law in 2022 after steep post-fire declines.

species.habitat: Breeds only at Melaleuca in south-west Tasmania; winters on saltmarsh along the Victorian and South Australian coast.
species.note: One of only three migratory parrots in the world. It crosses Bass Strait twice a year. In 2016 just three females returned to Tasmania to breed. Intensive captive release has lifted returning numbers back into the dozens.
threats: A migration that removes most first-year birds
Loss of coastal saltmarsh wintering habitat

pop.basis: Orange-bellied Parrot Recovery Team counts of birds returning to Melaleuca

species.habitat: Box-ironbark woodland of inland south-eastern Australia, following irregular eucalypt flowering.
species.note: Down to a few hundred birds, and now so sparse that young males cannot find adults to learn from — some have started singing the songs of other species instead. Captive-bred birds are taught the correct song from recordings before release.
threats: Loss of over 90% of box-ironbark woodland
Nest predation by noisy miners and currawongs
Loss of song culture in a sparse population

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Breeds in Tasmanian blue gum forest; migrates across Bass Strait to mainland box-ironbark woodland.
species.note: The fastest parrot in the world, reaching 88 km/h. Its Tasmanian nest hollows are raided by sugar gliders introduced to the island, which kill incubating females — modelling suggests the species could decline by 94% within three generations.
threats: Predation of nesting females by introduced sugar gliders
Logging of Tasmanian blue gum nesting forest
Loss of mainland winter feeding woodland

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Spinifex grassland on stony desert country in western Queensland and Western Australia.
species.note: For most of the twentieth century it was known only from two road-killed specimens and became the most sought-after bird in Australia. It was photographed alive for the first time in 2013. It roosts inside old spinifex hummocks and flies only in full darkness.
threats: Loss of long-unburnt spinifex to changed fire regimes

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Sphagnum bog and wet heath above 1,300 m in Kosciuszko National Park, New South Wales.
species.note: Jet black with bright yellow stripes, and one of very few vertebrates that manufactures its own alkaloid poison rather than acquiring it from food. Chytrid fungus reduced the wild population to a handful of animals; nearly all now alive are captive-bred and released into disease-free enclosures.
threats: The 2019-20 bushfires burning much of the remaining range
Fewer than 50 mature animals left in the wild

pop.basis: NSW Department of Planning and Environment Corroboree Frog Recovery Program counts

species.habitat: A few sandstone gorges in Wollemi National Park, New South Wales — the location is kept secret.
species.note: Known only from 200-million-year-old fossils until a park ranger abseiled into a gorge in 1994 and found a stand of living trees. Fewer than sixty adult trees survive in the wild. It was defended by helicopter-borne firefighters during the 2019-20 bushfires.
threats: Phytophthora root disease carried in on boots
Almost no genetic variation between individuals

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Sandy beaches and rocky islands along the coasts of South and Western Australia.
species.note: It has the strangest breeding cycle of any pinniped — a 17- to 18-month cycle that is out of phase between colonies, so pups are born at different times of year a few hundred kilometres apart. Most colonies number fewer than 50 pups.
threats: Extremely low genetic exchange between colonies

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment; South Australian and Western Australian pup production counts

species.habitat: Humid forest and maquis shrubland in the mountains of Grande Terre, New Caledonia.
species.note: Ash-grey, nearly flightless, with a shaggy crest it raises like a fan and blood-red legs. It is the only member of its family, with no close living relative anywhere. Pairs duet at dawn with a sound like a barking dog, audible over a kilometre.
threats: Predation by introduced dogs, cats, rats and pigs

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: Montane rainforest of the Torricelli Mountains in Sandaun Province, Papua New Guinea.
species.note: Also called Scott's tree kangaroo — a chocolate-brown, thick-tailed marsupial that climbs. It was down to about 100 animals when local villages agreed to a hunting moratorium in 2001, in exchange for water tanks and protein alternatives. Numbers have since risen several-fold.
threats: Hunting for meat, now under a community moratorium
Human population growth in surrounding villages

pop.basis: Tenkile Conservation Alliance village-based monitoring, Torricelli Mountains

species.habitat: Cloud forest above 1,000 m on the Huon Peninsula, Papua New Guinea.
species.note: Chestnut and gold, with a long tail used as a counterweight rather than a grasping limb. It is the flagship for the YUS Conservation Area, the first area in Papua New Guinea placed under legal protection by the landowners themselves.
threats: Conversion of cloud forest to gardens and coffee

pop.label: No total estimate; assessed as declining by more than 50% over three generations across the Huon Peninsula.

species.habitat: Limestone forest and scrub on Rota and Cocos Island, after extinction in the wild on Guam.
species.note: Wiped out on Guam by the introduced brown tree snake, which arrived after the Second World War and removed most of the island's forest birds. Declared Extinct in the Wild in 1987. Captive breeding and release on snake-free islands earned it a downlisting to Critically Endangered in 2019 — only the second bird ever to move back from Extinct in the Wild.
threats: The brown tree snake, which still prevents return to Guam

pop.basis: Guam Department of Agriculture and US Fish and Wildlife Service release-site monitoring

species.habitat: Four steep forested valleys on the island of Tahiti, French Polynesia.
species.note: Down to about a dozen adults in 1998. Rat and myna control, and the removal of invasive Miconia, have taken it past a hundred birds. Adults are glossy black; juveniles are cinnamon and take three years to darken.
threats: Predation by black rats and introduced common mynas
Invasive Miconia and Syzygium replacing native forest
A total range of four valleys

pop.basis: Société d'Ornithologie de Polynésie (MANU) annual territory census

species.habitat: Dry tropical forest on a handful of small islands in western Fiji, chiefly Yadua Taba.
species.note: Emerald green with narrow white bands and a low crest of spines. It changes to near-black when stressed. Yadua Taba holds almost the entire world population; the dry forest it needs is one of the most reduced habitats in the Pacific.
threats: Loss of dry tropical forest to fire and goats
Predation by introduced rats and cats
Invasive American iguanas competing on some islands
A world range of a few square kilometres

pop.basis: National Trust of Fiji Yadua Taba monitoring

species.habitat: Rainforest and coastal terrace of Christmas Island in the Indian Ocean.
species.note: The island's other native mammals are gone: two endemic rats and the Christmas Island pipistrelle are extinct, and its shrew has not been recorded since 1985. It pollinates and disperses the seeds of many of the island's native trees.
threats: Yellow crazy ants disrupting the forest ecosystem
A world population confined to one small island

pop.label: Roost counts suggest a few thousand animals and a decline of more than 35% in recent decades; the cause is not fully understood.

statusSource.text: Listed as Critically Endangered under Australia's Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999.
statusSource.iucnNote: the IUCN Red List includes it in Blyth's flying fox, Pteropus melanotus, assessed as Vulnerable in 2021

species.habitat: Warm open ocean and coastal aggregation sites in all tropical seas, feeding at plankton blooms.
species.note: The largest fish alive, up to 18 m, and a filter feeder that strains plankton through pads in its throat. The pattern of spots behind the gills is unique to each animal — the identification software used to match them was adapted from an algorithm for mapping star fields.
threats: Targeted fishing for fins and meat, mainly in South and Southeast Asia
Vessel strikes at coastal aggregation sites

pop.label: No global total. Indo-Pacific numbers have fallen by an estimated 63% and Atlantic numbers by around 30% over three generations.

species.habitat: The open ocean above 20 °C, usually in the top 150 m and far from land.
species.note: Once described as the most abundant large animal on Earth over 45 kg. Long, paddle-shaped white-tipped fins and an unhurried, curious manner. Its population has fallen by an estimated 98% in parts of its range — one of the steepest declines recorded for any large marine animal.
threats: Bycatch and finning in industrial tuna and swordfish longline fisheries
High value of its large fins
No effective enforcement across most of the high seas

pop.label: Global decline estimated at over 80%, with regional falls above 98% in the Gulf of Mexico and north-west Atlantic.

species.habitat: Coastal and semi-oceanic waters worldwide; forms enormous daytime schools at seamounts.
species.note: The wide head is a sensory instrument — it spreads electroreceptors over a broad sweep, letting the shark find rays buried in sand. Juveniles use shallow coastal nurseries, which puts them in exactly the water most heavily fished with gillnets.
threats: Fin trade — its fins are among the most valuable
Gillnet bycatch in coastal nursery grounds
Schooling behaviour that allows whole aggregations to be taken at once

pop.label: Estimated global decline of more than 80% over three generations; some regional populations have fallen over 95%.

species.habitat: Open ocean and productive coastal upwellings; visits reef cleaning stations across the tropics.
species.note: A wingspan of up to seven metres and the largest brain-to-body ratio of any fish. Mantas recognise themselves in mirrors, which very few non-mammals do. Females give birth to a single pup every two to three years.
threats: Targeted fishing for gill plates sold in Chinese medicine markets
Bycatch in purse-seine and gillnet fisheries
Disturbance and boat strikes at aggregation sites

pop.label: No global total; monitored subpopulations have declined by 50-95% and few number more than a thousand animals.

species.habitat: Temperate continental shelf waters; follows plankton fronts near the surface in summer.
species.note: The second-largest fish, up to 12 m, cruising with its mouth open to filter plankton through gill rakers. Basking sharks were hunted into the 20th century for liver oil — a single large animal could yield 2,000 litres. Some populations are now slowly recovering.
threats: Historic targeted fisheries for liver oil
Bycatch and entanglement in fixed gear

pop.label: No global total; the north-east Atlantic population is increasing under protection, while Pacific numbers remain very low.

species.habitat: Coral reef and rocky shore across the tropics; nests on small, often remote beaches.
species.note: Named for a narrow beak used to extract sponges from reef crevices — it is one of very few animals that eats sponges, and by doing so it keeps them from smothering coral. Its shell is the original tortoiseshell, and the trade in it killed millions of turtles.
threats: Historic and continuing trade in tortoiseshell
Loss of coral reef feeding habitat
Nesting beach development and light pollution

pop.label: Estimated global decline of more than 80% over three generations; roughly 20,000-23,000 females nest annually worldwide.

species.habitat: The open ocean from the tropics to sub-polar waters — the most widely distributed reptile on Earth.
species.note: The largest turtle, up to 900 kg, with no hard shell — a leathery ridged carapace over a layer of oily flesh. It maintains a body temperature well above the surrounding water and dives beyond 1,200 m. It eats almost nothing but jellyfish.
threats: Bycatch in longline and gillnet fisheries
Ingestion of plastic bags mistaken for jellyfish
Loss of nesting beaches; the Pacific subpopulations are Critically Endangered

pop.label: Globally Vulnerable, but the East and West Pacific subpopulations are separately Critically Endangered and have fallen by over 90%.

species.habitat: Temperate and subtropical seas; nests on beaches in the Mediterranean, Florida, Oman, Japan and Australia.
species.note: A heavy-headed turtle with jaws strong enough to crush conch and horseshoe crabs. Hatchlings from Japan cross the entire Pacific to Baja California and come back — a round trip of some 20,000 km — navigating by the Earth's magnetic field.
threats: Bycatch in longline, trawl and gillnet fisheries
Coastal development and lighting on nesting beaches
Sand temperature rise skewing hatchling sex ratios towards females

pop.label: Globally Vulnerable; the North Indian Ocean and South Pacific subpopulations are separately Critically Endangered.

species.habitat: Tropical open ocean and coastal waters; nests in mass arrivals on a few beaches in India, Costa Rica and Mexico.
species.note: The most abundant sea turtle, and still declining. It nests in arribadas — hundreds of thousands of females coming ashore over a few nights on the same stretch of sand, at Odisha, Ostional and Escobilla. So much of the species is concentrated in so few places that a single bad event matters enormously.
threats: Extreme concentration of nesting at a handful of sites

pop.label: Roughly 800,000 females nest annually, mostly at a few arribada beaches; the global trend remains downward.

species.habitat: Deep ocean worldwide, diving to 2,000 m and beyond in search of squid.
species.note: The largest toothed predator on Earth, with the biggest brain of any animal. It dives for over an hour at a time and hunts in total darkness by echolocation, producing clicks loud enough to be the loudest sound made by any animal. Family groups have distinct dialects of coded clicks.
threats: Historic whaling that removed an estimated two-thirds of the population

pop.basis: IUCN Red List global assessment; the pre-whaling population is estimated at around 1.1 million

species.habitat: Steep outer reef slopes and lagoons across the Indo-Pacific.
species.note: Up to two metres and 180 kg, with thick lips and a bulbous forehead that grows with age. All are born female; the largest become male. It is one of the few predators that eats crown-of-thorns starfish, and it is prized alive in the luxury live reef fish trade.
threats: The live reef food fish trade, which targets the largest individuals
Cyanide fishing to capture fish alive
Sex-changing biology that makes removal of large fish especially damaging

pop.label: No global total; densities have fallen by more than 50% across most of the range and it is absent from heavily fished reefs.

species.habitat: Coral reef throughout the Caribbean and the western Atlantic to Bermuda.
species.note: It gathers to spawn in the same places at the same full moons every year, in aggregations that once numbered tens of thousands. Fishers learned the dates. Most known aggregation sites are now gone, and the species has been lost from much of its range.
threats: Loss of most historical aggregation sites

pop.label: More than two-thirds of known spawning aggregations no longer form; the species has declined an estimated 60% over three generations.

species.habitat: The temperate Southern Ocean between 30° and 50° S; spawns only in the Indian Ocean south of Java.
species.note: Warm-blooded, capable of 70 km/h, and spawning in one place on Earth. Sustained overfishing cut the spawning stock to around 5% of its original size. A rebuilding plan agreed in 2011 has produced a genuine recovery, and in 2021 the IUCN downlisted it from Critically Endangered to Endangered.
threats: Historic and continued overfishing for the sashimi market
A single spawning ground south of Java

pop.label: The spawning stock is estimated at roughly 20% of its unfished size, up from around 5% at its lowest, and rebuilding under quota.

species.habitat: Gravel desert and sand plain of the Arabian Peninsula, where it can go weeks without drinking.
species.note: Extinct in the wild in 1972, when the last animal was shot in Oman. Nine survivors formed the 'World Herd' in Phoenix, and reintroduction began in 1982. In 2011 it became the first species ever to move from Extinct in the Wild all the way back to Vulnerable.
threats: Poaching and live capture for private collections
Small, managed populations dependent on supplementary water

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment

species.habitat: Steep desert escarpment and rocky wadi from the Negev and Sinai down the Red Sea coast to Yemen.
species.note: A small desert ibex, pale sand-coloured, with long swept-back ridged horns on males. It descends cliffs that look vertical to reach water at dawn, and it can tolerate body temperatures that would kill most mammals before it needs to drink.
threats: Competition with livestock at scarce waterholes

pop.basis: IUCN SSC Caprinae Specialist Group range-wide estimate

species.habitat: Breeds only in the reedbeds of the Mesopotamian Marshes of southern Iraq; winters in East African swamps.
species.note: Its entire breeding range is one wetland system, which was deliberately drained in the 1990s to around 10% of its extent, then partially reflooded after 2003. The bird's fortunes have followed the water level almost exactly.
threats: Drainage and upstream damming of the Mesopotamian Marshes
Loss of East African wintering wetlands

pop.basis: IUCN Red List assessment by BirdLife International

species.habitat: The Tigris-Euphrates river system and its marshes, from Anatolia to the Shatt al-Arab.
species.note: A large, flat, leathery-shelled turtle that lies buried in river mud with only its snorkel-like snout showing. Its river has been dammed more comprehensively than almost any other on Earth, and sandbank nesting sites have gone with the floods that built them.
threats: Killing by fishermen who regard it as a competitor

pop.label: No population estimate; the assessment records a decline of more than 50% over three generations across the basin.

species.habitat: Mountain forest between 1,300 and 2,000 m in Lebanon, western Syria and the Turkish Taurus.
species.note: The tree of the Phoenician fleet, Solomon's temple and the Lebanese flag. Exploited for five thousand years, it now survives in Lebanon as a dozen scattered groves; the largest remaining forests are in Turkey. Individual trees can exceed a thousand years.
threats: Millennia of logging leaving only fragments in Lebanon
A warming, drier climate pushing the viable zone uphill
Insect outbreaks linked to drought stress

pop.label: Lebanese groves total around 2,000 hectares of what was once a continuous mountain forest; Turkish stands are larger but also reduced.

species.habitat: Seagrass meadows and sandy seabed across the Mediterranean, anchored upright in the sediment.
species.note: The largest bivalve in the Mediterranean, up to 1.2 m tall, standing point-down in seagrass like a buried fan. It filters several thousand litres a day. From 2016 a parasite swept the basin and killed close to 100% of the population in most areas within three years.
threats: A Haplosporidium parasite that has caused near-total mortality basin-wide

pop.label: Mass mortality since 2016 has killed an estimated 80-100% of individuals across most of the Mediterranean; survivors are scattered and few.
